The White House nominated four individuals to fill vacant seats at the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, making the first such nominations in roughly a year.

Nathan Anonick of Virginia and Matthew Rowland of the District of Columbia were nominated to be commissioners of the CFTC. Kristin N. Johnson of Michigan and Steven Levine of Maryland were nominated to be members of the SEC.

The nominations are bipartisan — Anonick and Levine are Republicans; Johnson and Rowland are Democrats. The Senate Agriculture Committee will consider the CFTC nominees, while the Senate Banking Committee will consider the SEC nominees.

Anonick currently serves as legislative counsel to Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman and worked as a lead negotiator on the Agriculture Committee's portion of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. Rowland is a CFTC attorney who has been detailed to the Senate Agriculture Committee and also worked on the Clarity Act and the 2024 Agriculture Committee crypto bill.

Meanwhile, Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, focused on digital assets, risk management, and market integrity. Johnson has spoken often about crypto and the need for regulations around crypto asset custody, DeFi, and AI.

Levine most recently served as General Counsel and a senior advisor at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, and previously worked at the SEC as counsel and deputy chief of staff to Commissioner Mark Uyeda.

Levine was nominated to succeed Hester Peirce, a vocal advocate for the crypto industry who led the agency's Crypto Task Force and assisted Chairman Paul Atkins' Project Crypto to modernize securities regulation to accommodate crypto innovation and advance the goal of making the U.S. the "crypto capital of the world."

Ji Kim, chief executive of the Crypto Council for Innovation, congratulated the nominees in a post on X, stating that strong, bipartisan representation is essential to developing durable rules that safeguard markets, protect consumers, and support innovation.

"Both the CFTC and SEC will continue to play central and consequential roles in our financial markets, and together these nominees bring a wealth of experience and expertise that will help ensure continued American leadership," Kim wrote.

#5046. EU DeFi proposals could push users to riskier platforms, says Coinbase exec

Coinbase’s EU policy chief says applying suitability tests beyond crypto lending and borrowing could limit access and fragment liquidity.

European Union efforts to tighten oversight of decentralized finance (DeFi) could drive crypto users toward platforms offering fewer investor protections, according to Coinbase’s head of EU policy.

Roeland Van der Stappen told Cointelegraph that regulated crypto platforms could respond by limiting or dropping access to DeFi services.

“Rules designed to protect investors would end up pushing activity towards the places with the least protection,” Van der Stappen said.

In its September response to the European Commission’s consultation on the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), the European Securities and Markets Authority recommended creating a new category of regulated crypto services for firms that give customers access to DeFi protocols.

In September, the European Banking Authority (EBA) urged the Commission to study new rules for crypto lending and borrowing, including when regulated platforms give customers access to DeFi lending protocols. It listed suitability tests, which assess whether a service is appropriate for a customer, as one option in its consultation response.

Related: France proposes liability for crypto exchanges offering DeFi access

Van der Stappen said that extending such tests to other DeFi services could mean treating a simple stablecoin swap the same way as leveraged lending, despite their different risks.

Lending, liquidity provision and on-chain swaps would be the most exposed activities, he said. Some providers may narrow their offerings or even withdraw DeFi access altogether.

“A proportionate approach would be to allow CASPs [crypto-asset service providers] to continue offering that access with safeguards matched to the activity,” Van der Stappen said.

Van der Stappen said restricting access through regulated platforms could split DeFi liquidity into smaller pools and leave EU users with worse prices on trades.

He said the restrictions could encourage “walled gardens,” or isolated DeFi services, and steer users toward providers outside the EU with fewer safeguards.

A 2026 Adan-Ipsos survey found that 49% of French crypto buyers preferred accessing DeFi through exchanges, compared with 14% who favored personal wallets.

A Chainalysis report on Monday attributed a modest decline in crypto activity in Germany largely to declining decentralized exchange activity. Across the EU, crypto activity grew 2.2% in the 12 months through June 2026.

A 2025 Chainalysis report described DeFi as a small but growing segment of Europe’s crypto market. In the European Economic Area, May 2025 was the strongest month for DeFi lending activity in the period Chainalysis examined.

According to TRM's Thursday release, the company pointed out that many law enforcement agencies lack direct relationships or the capacity to package requests correctly and act while funds remain in motion. TRM said Beacon Concierge has already supported 15 cases for 14 agencies in 10 countries, with more than $35 million frozen. More than $200 million has been interdicted with Beacon members to date, the company added.

The company's own investigators assist agencies by tracing funds, preparing evidence packages, flagging addresses in the network, and supporting requests for freeze and seizure. Stablecoin issuers can freeze funds on-chain.

"Beacon Concierge puts our investigators, our tracing and the Beacon Network behind every verified agency, so more cases can move from first lead to issuer action."

TRM cited the Beacon Network's response to the Binance exploit as an illustration of the scale involved.

The network has labeled more than 26,000 addresses across 14 blockchains, traced more than 67,000 transfers and links, including over 1,050 cross-chain swaps. TRM said the network followed funds from 59 origin addresses an average of 10 hops and as far as 71.

Network members flagged 39% of the addresses, while Beacon identified the other 61% automatically from those flags. The network delivered more than 45,000 alerts to participating platforms, the company added.

"The Binance hack shows why cross-chain and multi-asset coordination is more important than ever," TRM said. "No investigator could have followed every branch by hand. Beacon Concierge is built so that any agency, not only those with a large team and an existing issuer relationship, can put that kind of coverage behind a case."

#5043. Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Bitcoin custody has always involved some degree of risk, but wallet manufacturers like Trezor—which build physical devices designed to keep a user’s private keys secure offline—are preparing for a post-quantum world where new challenges arise.

That’s because SHRINCS, the community’s leading candidate for a post-quantum signature scheme, allows users to make transactions using stateful signatures that require rigid state tracking to prevent funds from being stolen, according to Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka.

Proposed late last year by Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick and cryptographer Mikhail Kudinov, SHRINCS centers on a composite hash-based approach: users can make transactions using either stateful signatures or stateless signatures.

Stateless signatures are quite large—potentially affecting fees, signature speed, and other efficiency metrics—but are safe to reuse, while smaller, more efficient stateful signatures come with serious security risks when reused beyond a particular signing budget.

The stateful component of SHRINCS is made up of a tree of one-time signatures, and if these keys are accidentally used more than once, enough cryptographic information is revealed for someone else to forge that user’s signature and effectively steal funds.

If Bitcoin successfully adopts SHRINCS, maintaining a meticulous count of the wallet’s state will become a critical responsibility for wallet developers—with lots of potential edge-case security risks.

“You’re giving them an option to mess up,” Sušánka said during a recent episode of MARA Foundation TV, in reference to state tracking. “It’s our job to make it in a secure way, right? It shouldn't be the user’s job.”

To mitigate this risk, Trezor is weighing options for how to support secure UX in a post-quantum world. For instance, Sušánka said the company is considering making the heavier, slower stateless signatures the default setting for all users, tucking the riskier stateful option behind an advanced settings wall.

While Sušánka recognizes that SHRINCS may be the conservative cryptographic choice because it relies on the same cryptographic assumptions as SHA-256, he is “kind of torn on the topic because maintaining the state is a burden.”

“For example, you can have two Trezors with the same recovery seed. How do you share the state between those two? You really don’t,” he added.

“That being said, as it is with everything, this is about trade-offs,” Sušánka continued. “The [stateful] signatures are 10 times smaller ... That makes a big difference. So, I just don't want to throw it off the table completely.”

Sušánka went on to share that while many are focused on Bitcoin’s migration path to post-quantum addresses and signatures, hardware wallet devices will also need to be physically updated for full quantum protection. Most signing devices use quantum-vulnerable cryptography for hardware-specific security functions, like firmware and device authentication.

If users want to ensure their devices are secure in a post-quantum world, they will need to use “quantum-ready” devices—that is, devices that use post-quantum cryptography for device and firmware authentication as well.

In anticipation of these needs, the company is already shipping products like Trezor Safe 7 that support post-quantum cryptography for wallet authentication processes. Of course, transactions made on these devices will only be quantum-secure once Bitcoin itself upgrades to post-quantum security.

That said, Sušánka warned developers not to wait too long to give users migration options, as he believes the migration of potentially millions of users will take time.

“People should be ready to make compromises,” Sušánka said. “If we’re all going to be very strict on what can and cannot be done, we’re not going to get anywhere.”

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#5037. Are Alt-L1s over? Security, costs drive smaller chains to Ethereum

L1 blockchains Zilliqa, Gnosis and Ronin join the Ethereum ecosystem as the costs of going it alone grow, and the security and liquidity advantages become too hard to resist.

Running an independent blockchain has always come with a particular promise: control.

A standalone Layer 1 architecture allows projects to be the masters of their own destiny, set the rules of consensus, maintain their own validators and build infrastructure around their users, without relying on any other network.

But with great power comes great responsibility — and considerable expense.

Blockchains need enough users, developers and economic activity to support the infrastructure that secures them. For some smaller networks, keeping an entire ecosystem afloat no longer makes economic sense.

Zilliqa is the latest project to confront that reality, announcing plans last week to move away from its L1 architecture and become an Ethereum-based Layer 2 (L2) instead:

“Usage never reached what a standalone chain needs,” the post explained. “Funding and liquidity for standalone L1s dried up. The recent hacks showed how much it takes to secure a chain alone. The data is onchain for everyone to see.”

Blockchain ecosystem Gnosis (which has always been Ethereum-adjacent) is also working to transition Gnosis Chain into an Ethereum-based network through its Ethereum Economic Zone (EEZ) initiative. Its RollupX test network intends to show how participating chains can share Ethereum settlement and synchronous composability as native rollups.

Gaming-focused Ronin blockchain also completed its move back to Ethereum as an L2 in May.

With interest in alt L1s drying up along with the funding, will we start to see more and more chains consolidating in the Ethereum ecosystem?

Independent L1s generally have to keep several core functions going, including execution, consensus, data availability and settlement. They must also fund the token incentives used to secure their networks through staking.

Related: What are native rollups? Full guide to Ethereum’s latest innovation

“It comes down to a chain’s profitability,” Max Shannon, senior research analyst at Bitwise, tells Magazine.

ZIL becomes a Layer 2 on Ethereum. Source: Zilliqa

“L2s only need to maintain execution and do not necessarily need a token, which makes them a more attractive financial and operational proposition,” he says.

Shannon says the top ten largest projects are more financially sustainable. Coinbase and Robinhood’s L2 networks generated $48 million and $52 million in fees respectively over the last 365 days, with margins above 90%. The next eight largest chains each generated more than $1 million annually.

From 11th place onward, however, annual fees collectively amounted to less than $1 million. So a network may have ambitious technology and a dedicated community, but those things don’t necessarily pay the bills.

Ethereum is often criticized for giving away too much of its revenue to L2s, but that’s precisely what makes it attractive to set up projects there.

But just becoming an Ethereum L2 doesn’t automatically make a network profitable however. Shannon points to Optimism, Katana and Linea as examples of networks whose expenses outweigh their fee revenue. Projects like Blast have already been forced to shut down.

Gnosis has targeted spring 2027 to complete its transition, which will see it give up its independent validator-based consensus in favor of Ethereum settlement.

Gnosis Chain will relaunch as an Ethereum Economic Zone. Source: Gnosis

“Two years ago I gave a talk about ‘native Rollups’ that would truly extend Ethereum instead of being isolated chains,” co-founder Martin Köppelmann said, adding that RollupX “even goes beyond what I had imagined back then!”

Gnosis’s EEZ initiative aims to enable separate Ethereum-based networks interact synchronously, so a smart contract on one network can call another and use its response within the same transaction, without relying on the usual bridge-and-wait process.

That’s a prospect that has some Ethereum supporters particularly bullish, with ETH bull materkel describing the EEZ as a potential “black hole for liquidity,” and saying it could allow participating networks to tap into Ethereum’s total value locked (TVL) and strengthen its position as a liquidity hub.

Could network effects, and increased interoperability draw more and more chains into Ethereum’s orbit?

It isn’t only the operating cost economics that make sense. Projects can also tap into an established ecosystem of applications and developers rather than building those network effects from scratch.

Alex Gluchowski, co-founder and chief executive of Matter Labs, the company behind Ethereum L2 ZKsync, says he expects more L1 teams to maintain their own chains while using Ethereum for settlement.

“Running an independent L1 means maintaining its security as well as building something people want to use,” Gluchowski tells Magazine.

But Gluchowski says sovereignty and Ethereum integration are not mutually exclusive, since chains can retain control over their rules and operations while using Ethereum for shared settlement.

Ronin completed migration to Ethereum in May. Source: Ronin

And for applications handling sensitive financial information, maintaining a private environment under their own control can be essential, he says. Shared settlement does not have to mean exposing confidential transaction data.

The biggest obstacle today is that all the L2s are effectively isolated from each other and from Ethereum. It’s certainly possible to jump between them, but its far from seamless and interoperability is poor.

Shannon cautions against describing the market as undergoing straightforward consolidation around Ethereum.

Some large institutions are launching L2 networks, he says, including Coinbase and Robinhood, but others are still choosing to build independent L1s, like Circle’s Arc, Stripe’s Tempo, or Hyperliquid’s purpose-specific perpetual futures blockchain.

“So there is no clear conclusion to the L1 versus L2 debate as yet,” he says.

#5035. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

The DOJ and CFTC are asking the court to grant preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, arguing that Arkansas law is preempted by federal law and can't be enforced against CFTC-regulated prediction market platforms.

The Block has reached out to Kalshi and Griffin's office for comment.

The Arkansas dispute comes amid a growing wave of legal challenges against prediction market platforms across the U.S.

Also on Thursday, Louisiana became the latest state to take on those platforms, with Attorney General Liz Murrill also filing a lawsuit against companies including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, and Coinbase.

"For too long, they have violated our laws with impunity. No longer: I am seeking an immediate restraining order and an injunction to restore the rule of law in Louisiana," Murrill said in a post on X.

Last week, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction barring Kalshi from offering sports-event contracts on the lands of two California tribes — Blue Lake Rancheria and the Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians.

A Kalshi spokesperson said the company had voluntarily withdrawn its services from the tribes' lands in September.

#5027. Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

Crypto hackers stole $8.7 billion so far in 2026, surpassing the projected annual onchain revenue generated across the industry, according to ARK’s research director.

Hackers stole 57 cents for every $1 earned onchain by blockchain protocols since 2017, according to Lorenzo Valente, director of digital asset research at ARK Investment Management.

“Security is the bottleneck,” wrote Valente in a Thursday X post, sharing a chart showing that $8.7 billion lost to crypto hacks year to date had already surpassed the $5.6 billion in estimated annual onchain revenue for 2026.

Since 2017, the crypto industry has lost about $26.9 billion to hacks and earned $47 billion in total onchain revenue, he added.

The recent $6.3 billion stolen in the Binance hack alone exceeded Valente’s estimate for full-year 2026 onchain revenue. Value lost to hacks is on track to exceed onchain revenue by year-end for the first time since 2020.

The crypto industry saw a string of high-value hacks this year, including September’s $387 million Bitget hack and the $320 million Liquid Network exploit, as well as April’s $295 million Drift Protocol exploit.

The mounting security exploits are weighing on the institutional appetite for DeFi. In an April research note, JPMorgan analysts identified bridge security as a long-standing challenge for the industry.

Total value locked in decentralized finance (DeFi) has fallen nearly 10% since the Binance exploit, from $85.9 billion on Oct. 29 to $77.4 billion on Thursday, according to DefiLlama.

#5025. Thailand seeks $148,000 daily cap on certain stablecoin transfers to curb money laundering

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The draft rules would limit individual customers’ withdrawals and deposits at a single regulated digital asset venue to 5 million baht (approximately $147,750) per day.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking public comments on a draft notification that would limit stablecoin transfers to crack down on money laundering.

The proposal, announced Thursday, would limit individual customers' withdrawals and deposits on regulated digital asset venues to 5 million baht (approximately $147,750) per operator, in either direction, per day. The draft regulation follows a public hearing in September on supervising stablecoin activity through licensed operators.

Beyond the amount limit, the draft rules require that stablecoins be transferred only between accounts or wallets belonging to the same person and prohibit transfers involving another person's wallets. However, the rules do not cover pure peer-to-peer, onchain transactions outside of registered platforms.

The agency would also require operators to comply with the Travel Rule by conducting customer profiling and screening, and use blockchain analytics tools to identify links to high-risk or watchlisted wallets.

“The value of stablecoins transferred into and out of a customer’s account must be commensurate with the customer’s source of income and financial position," the SEC stated.

Meanwhile, certain transfers would be exempt from the 5 million baht limit, such as movements between a customer’s own accounts on platforms under the SEC’s supervision, transfers by operators themselves for business purposes, stablecoin market-maker activity, and specific transactions related to digital token offerings and refunds. Certain activities approved by the Bank of Thailand will also be exempt from the limit.

These draft rules aim to prevent digital assets from being used for money laundering, cybercrime, or circumventing rules on international money transfers, the SEC stated.

The draft also introduces additional measures. Crypto exchanges would be required to disclose the names of their market makers and the assets for which they provide liquidity, along with enhanced screening of those firms.

Furthermore, brokers would be barred from using liquidity providers for stablecoin-baht trading pairs. Off-platform transactions by brokers and dealers would be subject to a minimum threshold of 3 million baht ($88,528), and operators would have to disclose the trading prices for such deals.

The SEC is currently seeking public comments on the draft notification, with Nov. 26 as the deadline.

The requirement builds on steps Thai authorities had already taken. The country’s central bank and securities regulator had reportedly started using data analytics to scrutinize unusual USDT trading, as part of a wider push to close gaps that enable money laundering and other “grey economy” activity.

#5023. Thailand proposes $148K daily cap on stablecoin deposits and withdrawals

Thailand’s SEC would set separate daily caps for stablecoin deposits and withdrawals and require customers to use wallets they own.

Thailand’s securities regulator has proposed capping daily stablecoin deposits and withdrawals at 5 million baht ($148,000) each per customer at regulated crypto operators.

The limit would apply separately to deposits and withdrawals at each operator, Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said in a Thursday announcement. The regulator said the rules aim to curb money laundering, cybercrime and attempts to bypass cross-border money transfer rules.

The draft would bar stablecoin transfers to and from third-party wallets. Operators would have to verify that customers own the accounts or wallets they use for deposits and withdrawals.

Operators would have to comply with the Travel Rule, which requires crypto service providers to collect and share information about transfers, and use blockchain analytics to identify wallets linked to suspicious activity.

The draft would require crypto exchanges to name their market makers and identify the assets for which they provide liquidity. Crypto brokers would be barred from using liquidity providers for stablecoin-baht pairs. Certain off-platform trades would be subject to a 3 million baht minimum.

The draft follows a September consultation in which the SEC proposed stablecoin transfer limits and tighter oversight of crypto operators.

#5022. North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korean hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using a social-engineering scheme built on secretly recorded footage and AI deepfakes, the U.S. Justice Department said Thursday, as it announced the seizure of the infrastructure behind the operation.

The scheme, which the FBI calls “FaceStealer,” turns video conference calls into a trap. According to the DOJ, hackers lure targets into meetings using accounts stolen from previous victims, then play prerecorded webcam footage of trusted contacts to simulate their presence and win the target’s confidence.

The group also generates deepfake videos of well-known figures in the crypto and related industries, using AI to make the ruse more convincing.

Once a target is at ease, the attackers manufacture a fake technical glitch, such as claiming the person can’t be heard, and offer a link to “fix” it, which instead installs malware.

From there, the hackers can drain crypto wallets or exploit the victim’s access to other systems, sometimes waiting months or more than a year before striking. The FBI said it seized over 900 webcam recordings of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant.

The DOJ tied the operation to North Korean groups known variously as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among others, and warned the hackers have increasingly targeted open-source software developers in an apparent bid to enable supply-chain attacks.

The announcement came paired with an update on the record-breaking Binance hack. The department said it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen from the exchange on Oct. 29, part of over $2.7 billion frozen so far.

The FBI attributed that theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and the regime has been laundering the proceeds at speed, spinning up a new wallet roughly every 25 seconds. North Korea has denied involvement, calling the FBI’s finding a political provocation.

The actions underscore how central crypto theft has become to Pyongyang’s finances. The U.S. recently sanctioned 11 people over a North Korean IT-worker scheme that moved millions in crypto, and researchers have cataloged the many ways the regime’s hackers break into crypto firms.

Officials said efforts to trace and recover the stolen Binance funds are ongoing.

#5018. UK, Singapore, and Thailand central banks complete foreign exchange settlement trial linking traditional and tokenized systems

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas participated as observers, while the Bank of England plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028.

Three central banks have completed tests of a cross-border foreign exchange settlement system connecting traditional payment infrastructure with distributed ledger technology.

In a joint statement on Friday, the Bank of England, Monetary Authority of Singapore, and Bank of Thailand said they conducted the experiments using a prototype developed by Partior, which coordinated payment-versus-payment (PvP) settlement and multilateral net FX transactions across their test environments.

The three central banks are working under Project Meridian FX APAC, announced last November. The project encompassed multiple currencies, technologies, settlement infrastructures, and time zones, with the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas also participating as observers, the banks said.

According to the statement, Partio's system matched settlement instructions, coordinated the reservation of funds, monitored payment readiness, and initiated settlement.

The experiment also examined multilateral netting, which allows banks to offset payments against one another to reduce the liquidity needed for settlement.

However, the accompanying policy report identified questions around operational resilience, settlement finality, governance, liability, and cross-border data sharing. It also warned that additional functions, including holding funds or calculating net positions, could change an operator's regulatory responsibilities.

Tom Mutton, the BOE's executive director of payments, innovation and fintech, said the project provided "practical evidence of how synchronized settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions."

The BOE plans to launch a live synchronization interface in 2028. Findings from Project Meridian FX APAC will inform further work on synchronized settlement.

#5015. Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Josh Hawley wants Congress to hit the brakes on new data centers, just as lawmakers are moving forward with legislation intended to make building the infrastructure behind America's AI boom easier.

The Missouri senator called for a nationwide moratorium Wednesday, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans during the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks?” Hawley wrote on X. His answer included a moratorium on data centers, alongside defunding Planned Parenthood, suspending the gas tax and other Republican priorities.

A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a “bill of rights giving taxpayers guarantees of no rate increases.” Hawley has not presented detailed legislation specifying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last.

Data centers are the warehouses packed with powerful computers that train and operate services such as ChatGPT. Building more AI systems means installing more servers, which requires additional electricity, cooling equipment and often upgrades to local power grids.

Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go:DEFUND Planned ParenthoodMORATORIUM on data centersSUSPEND the gas tax FUND rural hospitals SAVE AMERICA ACT

— Josh Hawley (@HawleyMO) November 11, 2026

The scale helps explain the concern. U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, according to figures cited by Pew, and that could climb to 426 by 2030. In other words, their annual electricity demand could more than double in six years.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and President Donald Trump's administration.

The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines, helping bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those expenses onto ordinary electricity customers.

In practical terms, Congress is considering how to keep construction moving without making households subsidize it. Hawley is asking lawmakers to stop new construction until consumer protections are in place.

His position is not entirely new. In February, Hawley introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, seeking to make new data centers obtain electricity from their own sources rather than relying on existing grid supplies.

He now joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly supporting a national pause. Their moratorium proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers and public safety as well as the environment.

The politics have shifted quickly. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on data center development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction.

A Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday found 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats. Another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them.

Opponents worry about rising bills, water consumption and noise. Cities have already imposed restrictions, while OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates.

Industry supporters see a bigger economic risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment now depends on AI infrastructure.

A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity that AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. Existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined.

Hawley's call does not freeze a single project, and he has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill. For now, the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals, not legislation to ban new data centers.

#5014. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, exits board; shares plunge

Colette Kress will remain Nvidia’s chief financial officer while serving as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent successor.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president and CEO and stepped down from the company’s board on Thursday, effective immediately. The board named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

Kress will retain her role as CFO while Nvidia’s board considers internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO role. The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones its first chair and said it expects Nvidia’s operations to proceed without interruption.

Nvidia shares fell more than 13% shortly after the US market opened on Thursday, trading at $151.00 as of 2:31 p.m. UTC, according to Yahoo Finance. Bitcoin (BTC) fell alongside Nvidia shares, dropping as much as 3.5% to a multimonth low.

The shares later pared losses to trade at $165 at 4:24 p.m. UTC, down 5% on the day. The stock was down more than 26% over the previous month.

Kress has served as Nvidia’s CFO since September 2013 and previously held finance positions at Cisco and Microsoft.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter financial results on Nov. 17.

Huang’s departure comes just four days after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation amid reports that the company’s co-founder had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The board said it had no reason to believe US national security or Nvidia’s confidential information had been compromised, but would examine all available information.

In a separate message to employees that day, Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologized to his family and colleagues. He also pledged to cooperate with the investigation.

The Associated Press identified the woman involved in the affair as Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had concluded she was passing information to Beijing. China has denied targeting Huang.

On Tuesday, Nvidia’s independent directors retained former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the inquiry.

On Wednesday, reports said Nvidia’s board was preparing to remove Huang as CEO.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as its CEO for more than 33 years, overseeing its transformation from a graphics-chip maker into a leading supplier of AI processors. His departure marks the first CEO transition in the company’s history.

Nvidia’s market capitalization surged from approximately $57.5 billion at the end of 2016 to a peak of $5.5 trillion on Sept. 1, 2026, a nearly 96-fold increase, according to data from Stock Analysis.

Amid Nvidia’s sell-off, Huang’s estimated net worth fell to $140.6 billion as of 3:42 p.m. UTC Thursday from $162.2 billion on Nov. 9.

House lawmakers still want to question Jensen Huang about his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage, Rep. John Moolenaar said Thursday.

“We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us,” Moolenaar told reporters, according to Politico.

Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, and fellow committee chairs Rick Crawford and Brian Mast first requested a closed-door briefing in a Nov. 4 letter. They cited concerns about Beijing’s access to sensitive US technology and information and asked Huang to confirm by Nov. 11 whether he could attend on Nov. 18 or to propose another date.

Moolenaar said the lawmakers were prepared to subpoena Huang if they could not agree on a date. He also wants to determine whether Chinese intelligence gained access to sensitive information and examine Huang’s lobbying to ease US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he was considering forming a subcommittee to investigate the matter when the new Congress convenes in January.

#5012. From $6 to $6.9 million: Two dormant Bitcoin addresses wake up to move 100 BTC after more than 16 years

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The two sends took place just over two minutes apart, and a later transaction combined coins from both transfers into a single address.

Two Bitcoin addresses that had sat dormant for more than 16 years moved 100 BTC on Friday morning, worth approximately $6.89 million, according to onchain data.

The first address sent nearly 50 BTC to one address and 0.01 BTC to another at 4:08 a.m. UTC. Just over two minutes later, the second address sent nearly 49 BTC to one address and 1 BTC to another. Both sets of coins came from block rewards mined in September 2010, data from blockchain explorer Mempool shows. Onchain monitoring platform Whale Alert first reported the moves, estimating that each 50 BTC reward was worth about $3 when received in 2010.

By 4:48 a.m. UTC, about 20 BTC from the first transfer and 39 BTC from the second had been consolidated at a new address starting "bc1qj5." Some 30 BTC sits at another new address starting "bc1qqs," 10 BTC at "bc1qds," and 1 BTC at "bc1qce" at the time of writing.

The reason for the transfers, the identity of the wallets' owners, and whether the two original outputs had the same owner remain unknown.

With bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) currently trading for around $69,000, according to The Block's prices page, the value of the bitcoin the addresses transferred has risen more than 1.15 million times since 2010.

Mempool labels both 50 BTC inputs as pay-to-public-key, or P2PK. The four addresses that received the coins on Friday all start with bc1q, a prefix used by newer native SegWit (P2WPKH) addresses. Older Bitcoin addresses include pay-to-public-key-hash (P2PKH) addresses starting with 1 and pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) addresses starting with 3. The latest Taproot (P2TR) address format starts with bc1p.

Other early bitcoin holdings have moved to newer address formats after years of dormancy, and several addresses named in a New York lawsuit over allegedly abandoned bitcoin have moved funds recently after the plaintiffs sent onchain notices.

Five 50 BTC block rewards mined in April 2010 went untouched for about 15 years before they moved to two SegWit addresses in July 2025. The coins were worth about $29.6 million at the time. A March 2024 transaction combined 40 mining rewards from 2010, totaling 2,000 BTC worth nearly $140 million.

Ethereum is a Layer 1 blockchain designed for programmable applications. It uses accounts, smart contracts, the Ethereum Virtual Machine, ETH, gas fees, and Proof of Stake to support decentralized applications and compete within a wider ecosystem of Layer 1 blockchains.

While Bitcoin is viewed as digital gold, an inflation hedge, or digital money, other crypto entrepreneurs wanted to push the envelope further. A few years after Bitcoin, Ethereum outlined infrastructure for smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new financial systems. This guide explains Ethereum’s premise, ecosystem, advantages, and the hurdles Layer 1 blockchains face.

The lesson summaries below give a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Ethereum & Layer 1s 101 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Positions Ethereum as the next step after Bitcoin, adding smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new approaches to Layer 1 design.

Explains how Ethereum made blockchains programmable through smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Covers externally owned accounts, contract accounts, account balances, Bitcoin’s UTXO contrast, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

Shows how Ethereum supports automated financial services such as trading, lending, borrowing, and collateral management.

Introduces ETH, gas, gwei, network congestion, base and priority fees, and the role of EIP-1559.

Explains Ethereum’s move away from Proof of Work and the roles of validators, staking, and slashing.

Lesson 6 - Ethereum Improvement Proposals

Describes how EIPs move from a documented idea through public review and possible network implementation.

Compares Ethereum with other Layer 1 and Layer 0 designs through the blockchain trilemma.

Connects native tokens and blockspace to validator incentives, wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and other Web3 infrastructure.

Introduces the scalability problem and explains why Layer 2 systems are the natural next topic.

Bitcoin proved that a decentralized network could maintain money and a transaction ledger without a central authority. Ethereum extended that idea by making the blockchain programmable. Instead of only transferring value, Ethereum made it possible to run code on-chain.

The core innovation is the smart contract: a piece of code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when specific conditions are met. In the vending-machine analogy, you insert money, and the machine dispenses your snack without needing human intervention.

Smart contracts make decentralized applications, or dApps, possible. These applications function without traditional intermediaries, with use cases that range from financial services to games.

To understand how a vending machine can live inside a blockchain, start with Ethereum’s accounts. Ethereum has two main account types. Externally owned accounts, or EOAs, are user-controlled accounts secured by a private key. They can send and receive ETH, interact with smart contracts, and initiate transactions.

Contract accounts are controlled by smart-contract code, not private keys. They cannot initiate transactions on their own. Instead, they act in response to transactions sent by EOAs or other contracts, executing predefined code when triggered.

Ethereum also uses an account-based model, where balances are stored directly in accounts, similar to a bank ledger. This differs from Bitcoin’s UTXO model, which tracks individual transaction outputs. The account-based approach makes it easier for smart contracts to check balances and interact with users or other contracts.

Smart contracts execute inside a virtual environment called the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM. The EVM resembles a universal translation service: just as a translation service helps everyone in a multilingual meeting understand the same message, the EVM provides a framework where smart contracts run the same way on every node in the network.

That consistency matters because every participating node needs to agree on what the smart contract did. Ethereum’s application-focused account model and the EVM together power decentralized applications, including the broader ecosystem of decentralized finance.

Ethereum’s infrastructure was not set up this way by accident. The aim was to go beyond decentralized money and expand how financial services could work. This is where decentralized finance, or DeFi, comes in.

DeFi aims to replace or rework financial functions such as lending, borrowing, trading, and earning interest with blockchain-based protocols. Instead of relying on a bank or broker, users interact with smart contracts that enforce rules automatically.

ETH, or Ether, is the fuel or incentive that powers the Ethereum network. Every interaction, from sending tokens to deploying smart contracts, requires ETH to pay gas fees.

Gas fees are the cost that comes with every transaction or interaction with a smart contract. They serve two main purposes: they compensate validators for keeping the network running, and they help prevent spam by making every action on the network carry a cost.

Gas fees work like a toll system. Ethereum has limited blockspace, and when more users want to use the network at the same time, the cost of getting into the next block can rise.

Gas prices are commonly quoted in gwei. Under EIP-1559, a transaction fee includes a network-determined base fee and may include a priority fee for the validator. This gives users a clearer fee structure, although the total cost still changes with demand and the amount of computation required.

Ethereum initially operated with Proof of Work, where miners validate transactions by solving complex computational puzzles. It later transitioned to Proof of Stake in the upgrade known as The Merge.

Proof of Stake works differently. Instead of miners competing with hardware, validators are selected to create new blocks, with their role tied to ETH staked as collateral. Staking acts as a financial commitment to follow the rules, because dishonest behavior can put a validator’s staked funds at risk through slashing.

Ethereum Improvement Proposals, or EIPs, are formal proposal documents that describe potential changes to the Ethereum network. They resemble blueprints for upgrading a city bridge: an idea is written down, reviewed, debated, and, if accepted, implemented as a network upgrade.

Ethereum was one of the first major highways built for smart contracts, but as more people used it, traffic jams and higher tolls became common. That opened the door for other blockchain platforms to emerge with different design choices.

Chains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are called Layer 1 chains because they are base, independent networks that do not rely on another blockchain for operation. Other Layer 1s may optimize for speed, cost, decentralization, developer experience, or specific use cases.

The common challenge is the blockchain trilemma: improving two of the major cornerstones often comes at the cost of the third.

Layer 1 tokens such as ETH are not only traded assets. They play operational roles in paying for blockspace, incentivizing validators, and securing the network through rewards and fees.

Other important topics include Web3 infrastructure: wallets as user access points, middleware such as RPC nodes and oracles, and security/audit services that help applications interact with blockchain networks. These surrounding tools fill needed roles around the base blockchain.

Balancing the blockchain trilemma is difficult. To support broader adoption, scalability becomes a critical problem: without effective scaling solutions, blockchains can become too slow or too expensive for everyday use.

In a city-road analogy, a single-lane road works when only a few people drive, but if everyone starts driving at once, the road becomes gridlocked. Blockchains face a similar challenge when demand rises faster than the base layer can process activity.

Ethereum expanded blockchain use cases by introducing smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Ethereum uses EOAs, contract accounts, an account-based model, and the EVM to make smart-contract execution consistent across the network.

ETH is the native currency used to pay gas fees, which price computation and help prevent spam.

Proof of Stake replaces miners with validators who stake ETH and can be penalized for dishonest behavior.

EIPs provide a structured way to propose and coordinate Ethereum upgrades.

Alternative Layer 1s make different trade-offs across decentralization, scalability, and security.

Scaling is the natural next topic because base-layer blockchains face throughput and cost limits as adoption grows.

This 101 subject is designed for readers who already have a basic grasp of Bitcoin and blockchain terminology. It helps to understand what a blockchain is, why decentralization matters, how wallets and private keys work, and why blockchains need consensus before moving into Ethereum and Layer 1 design.

Ethereum: A Layer 1 blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Layer 1: A base blockchain network that does not rely on another chain for its core operation.

Smart contract: Code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when conditions are met.

dApp: A decentralized application that uses smart contracts instead of relying only on traditional intermediaries.

EOA: An externally owned account controlled by a private key.

Contract account: An Ethereum account controlled by smart-contract code.

EVM: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, where smart-contract logic executes consistently across the network.

Gas fee: The cost paid in ETH to process a transaction or smart-contract interaction.

Gwei: A small unit of ETH used to price gas.

Proof of Stake: A consensus model where validators stake ETH and participate in block creation and validation.

Slashing: A penalty mechanism that can reduce a validator’s stake for dishonest or faulty behavior.

EIP: An Ethereum Improvement Proposal describing a possible network change.

Blockchain trilemma: The trade-off among decentralization, scalability, and security.

Web3 infrastructure: Wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and related services that help users and applications interact with blockchains.

After Ethereum & Layer 1s, useful next topics include Scaling & Layer 2s, DeFi, Market Structure and the deeper Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 guide.

#5007. Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, widening a congressional inquiry that has moved from Huang's private life to U.S. controls on chip exports to China. "The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote in a tweet announcing the requests on Thursday evening.

In a letter dated November 12, Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3 over public reports that "raise significant national security concerns." The committee has jurisdiction over export controls, "including their application to NVIDIA's exports of advanced semiconductors," he wrote. If Huang does not appear, the committee "is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas."

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Scott asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting Commerce's "central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations." A Lutnick spokesperson told NBC News that he had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily," while the White House said President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence" in Lutnick.

Separately on Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees, Reps. Brian Mast (R-FL), John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR), wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department's under secretary for industry and security.

Huang was asked to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter on December 2, with each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena. Kessler, whose bureau administers export controls, was invited to a hearing on December 3.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three chairs said in a statement. They called on Congress to add four chip security bills to the annual defense authorization bill.

It is their second request. A letter dated November 4 had asked Huang to brief the committees on November 18. Mast told reporters on Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, NBC News reported.

At the center of the inquiries is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials suspected the company of helping Chinese firms get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, The New York Times reported in October. Its sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times.

Megaspeed told the Times it had hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws, according to NBC News.

The Times reported that U.S. officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has rejected that as a smear, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy, according to BBC News.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife and resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Moolenaar told reporters that Huang had "been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls," Roll Call reported. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records on Nvidia chip exports to China.

China's foreign ministry warned on Friday that tighter U.S. export controls on semiconductors would threaten the stability of global supply chains, Al Jazeera reported.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% at $166.19 on Thursday and were up 2.7% at $170.63 in premarket trading early on Friday, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company has lost almost $500 billion in market value since the close on Friday, November 6. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.

#5004. DTCC Plans Solana Expansion as Wallet Rules Limit Access

The US securities clearinghouse plans to bring tokenized stocks to Solana in 2027, but analysts say restrictions could limit adoption.

Plans by the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation’s (DTCC) to bring tokenized securities to Solana could attract more traditional financial institutions to the blockchain, but regulatory restrictions may limit the impact on the network, according to analysts.

DTCC announced Thursday that it plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027. The move would allow certain securities held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be turned into digital tokens on the network.

Solana is a blockchain known for its fast transactions and low fees, making it popular for crypto trading, especially memecoins. The network had about $4.94 billion in total value locked (TVL) as of Nov. 12, according to DefiLlama.

Experts say the move could help Solana attract more activity beyond just memecoins, but it’s not clear how much new capital and transaction volume it could bring to the network. What’s more, current US regulatory rules still limit who can hold and transfer the tokenized assets.

Alex Lin, founding partner at venture capital firm Reforge, said Solana’s history of handling large amounts of memecoin trading may have helped show that the network can support traditional financial activity.

“Memes were a public stress test that gave Solana credibility that it can handle retail-scale volume cheaply and reliably,” Lin told Cointelegraph. “The casino paved the way for more institutional plumbing.”

However, under a December 2025 SEC no-action letter, DTC participants must register wallets to hold tokenized securities. The tokens can only be transferred between registered wallets, potentially limiting usage.

“It’s overstated in the near term because the SEC relief from Dec 2025 keeps these tokens in a walled garden of registered DTC participants, so permissionless retail and DeFi liquidity can’t touch these tokens directly yet,” Lin said. “Regulators need to let these assets work as true onchain collateral and that’s more policy than tech.”

DTCC launched its tokenization service on the Canton Network and its private Besu network on Oct. 28, allowing certain securities to be turned into digital tokens while keeping the same investor protections. At launch, DTCC said 20 DTC participants had signed agreements to access the service, but it has not said whether any plan to use Solana.

Cointelegraph contacted DTCC and the Solana Foundation for additional comments but has not yet heard back.

Related: Robinhood’s Tenev warns US tokenization uncertainty deters ‘serious assets’

Kha Nguyen, CEO and co-founder of blockchain analytics platform Birdeye, which tracks trading activity on Solana, said the blockchain has already seen growing demand for tokenized stocks without DTCC’s involvement.

According to Birdeye’s H1 2026 report, tokenized-stock trading volume on Solana reached around $4.9 billion in the first half of the year, more than six times the volume recorded in the previous six months.

Birdeye’s third-quarter report also found that more than 1 million accounts held tokenized stocks on Solana by late September.

Still, broader trading activity on Solana has slowed with the network recording about 6.9 billion transactions in the 30 days ending Nov. 11, down almost 40% from the previous 30-day period, according to Token Terminal data. Meanwhile, trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) fell 34.4% to $39.1 billion, while monthly active addresses dropped nearly 13% to 45.8 million.

Network fees also fell 39% to about $17 million over the same period. However, the value of tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) on Solana rose almost 7% to $4.76 billion as of Nov. 11 – up from $4.46 billion on Oct. 12.

“By late September more than a million wallets had held a tokenized stock, and real-world assets on Solana had grown five times in a year,” Nguyen told Cointelegraph.

Nguyen said bringing more tokenized securities onto the network does not automatically mean more transactions or greater demand for Solana’s native cryptocurrency, SOL. “A trade is one transaction whether it moves $100 or $100 million,” Nguyen said. “What matters is turnover, not value parked on-chain.”

Nguyen said DTCC’s integration would need support from banks and other financial firms to have a real impact on Solana. Institutions would also need enough liquidity to support large trades.

“Banks, brokers and issuers need to say they will issue, trade and settle there, and then do it,” Nguyen said. He added that institutions would need to actively use the tokenized securities rather than simply hold them.

“The assets must be active, not idle: traded around the clock, used as collateral to borrow against, and earning yield,” Nguyen said.

Lin agreed that the longer-term impact would depend on how the assets are used, rather than which blockchain they are issued on.

“No one cares where the assets are issued, but more so where they’re used,” Lin said. “It’s all about where secondary trading and collateral activity will happen and ultimately settle.”

#5002. US Justice Department, business groups and DeFi firms challenge Illinois crypto tax

Industry groups argued in court filings that Illinois’ crypto tax, which applies even when a transaction yields no profit, could raise compliance costs and violate federal law.

The US Department of Justice, business and financial industry groups and a coalition of decentralized finance (DeFi) firms have backed a legal challenge to Illinois’ 0.2% digital asset tax, arguing that the measure unfairly targets cryptocurrency transactions and could impose taxes even when investors make no profit.

Over the past week, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest, while the US Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) submitted an amicus filing. A coalition that includes venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Paradigm as well as crypto protocols Uniswap and Aave Labs also filed a brief, according to a Thursday announcement from the Blockchain Association and Crypto Council for Innovation.

The law, enacted in June, imposes a 0.2% tax on the value of digital assets exchanged, transferred or stored, regardless of whether a transaction generates a profit.

The Digital Chamber sued Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and state revenue official David Harris in July, followed by a separate challenge from the Blockchain Association and Crypto Council for Innovation in August. Originally scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, the tax was delayed until July 1, 2027, allowing more time for the legal challenges.

Illinois had projected the digital asset tax would generate $60 million in fiscal year 2027 revenue, according to estimates from the governor’s budget office. Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch previously promoted the measure as part of a broader affordability agenda aimed at “closing corporate loopholes and making big tech companies and crypto billionaires pay their fair share,” the Chicago Tribune reported in July.

Lawmakers involved in advancing the legislation and the governor’s office did not respond to Cointelegraph’s requests for comment before publication.

Related: France advances stablecoin tax, eyes self-custodial wallets and exit tax proposals

In a Nov. 6 court filing, SIFMA and the US Chamber of Commerce warned that Illinois’ tax would affect banks, broker-dealers, custodians and asset managers across the country, potentially exposing them to significant compliance costs. They also highlighted the financial burden on customers.

“This means that a customer who loses money owes the same tax as a customer who earns a profit,” the filing said. “And a customer who moves the same asset between two accounts faces tax (potentially on both ends) without a sale, a gain, or a change in beneficial ownership.”

The groups said firms would need to develop systems to identify Illinois customers, value digital assets and determine which transactions are taxable, while facing potential criminal penalties for violations.

They also argued that the tax discriminates against digital asset services because comparable transactions involving traditional assets are not taxed in the same way, potentially violating federal internet tax protections and constitutional requirements for interstate commerce and uniform taxation.

The Justice Department also weighed in on Nov. 6, saying that Illinois’ digital asset tax undermines federal efforts to promote cryptocurrency innovation and US leadership in the sector.

The filing cited the creation of a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and the GENIUS Act, which established federal rules for stablecoins. The DOJ argued that less favorable tax treatment for digital assets could conflict with those policies.

Separately, the DeFi coalition warned about who could be held responsible for collecting the tax. In a Nov. 11 filing, the group argued that Illinois’ proposed rules could impose obligations on software developers and other blockchain participants who lack customer information, control over user funds or the ability to collect taxes.

#5001. Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Leading cryptocurrency Bitcoin has dropped 5.6% on the day, and is currently trading at just over $69,300, per Decrypt data. It comes after the latest consumer price index, or CPI, results came in "hotter than expected," experts said, with the drop was triggered by a "concentrated liquidation."

Bitcoin's plunge took it to a 24-hour low of $67,922, its lowest level since mid-August, when it boosted from $63,000.

"Bitcoin’s drop below $69,000 was directly triggered by a concentrated liquidation of leveraged long positions," Tim Sun, senior analyst at Hashkey, told Decrypt. "Though the deeper issue lies in steadily weakening market demand."

Sun highlighted U.S. Bitcoin spot ETFs recording six consecutive days of net outflows, according to CoinGlass. He also pointed to stablecoin supply shrinking and MSCI removing digital asset treasury firm Strategy from its funds.

"ETFs, stablecoin liquidity, and corporate treasuries have served as the primary capital pillars supporting this Bitcoin rally," Sun said. "With all three coming under simultaneous pressure, the market is losing the marginal buying power that previously propelled prices higher."

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies have also taken a hit. Ethereum has dropped 4.6% on the day to $1,953, BNB has slipped 4.7% to $639.46, and Solana is down 3.1% to $80.47, according to Decrypt data. The global crypto market cap has dropped 4.6% over the past 24 hours to $2.39 trillion.

It follows U.S. CPI rising 0.4% in October, which is "hotter than expected, even if the headline monthly rate eased to 0.4% from September’s 0.6%," according to CoinShares head of research James Butterfill. "More troubling was the composition," he added. "Food rose 0.5%, services remained firm, and core CPI increased 0.3%, with services excluding rent, a gauge of domestic price pressure the Fed watches closely, rising 0.5%. The inflation problem is therefore no longer easily dismissed as an oil story."

The consumer price index, or CPI, is a way of measuring inflation that tracks the average price changes of everyday goods and services over time. Central banks tend to use CPI to inform whether they'll cut or hike interest rates, meaning higher-than-expected CPI signals a potential Federal Reserve hike.

Polymarket predictors put a 97% chance on the Fed raising interest rates this year, up from 75% at the start of the week. The CME FedWatch tool, meanwhile, sees an 88% chance of a 25 basis point hike, with 12% anticipating a 50 basis point rise.

On top of the CPI, Bitcoin's downward move comes following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company, after reports of multiple affairs including with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive spread.

Huang's departure has sparked "severe volatility across tech stocks, further dampening market risk appetite," Sun told Decrypt. "This has prompted broader portfolio de-risking, amplifying the downward pressure on Bitcoin," he added.

For a crypto rebound to happen, Sun said that Bitcoin needs "long-term allocation capital" to flow back into crypto after ETFs, stablecoins, and digital asset treasury companies have taken a hit in recent weeks.

#4998. Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Strategy shares declined Thursday following MSCI’s decision to remove the company from its indexes, as Bitcoin also fell amid a broader crypto market decline.

Shares of Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin treasury company Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday, closing at $114.41, a day after MSCI confirmed the company’s removal from its global equity indexes and amid a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off.

On Wednesday, MSCI confirmed that Strategy would be removed from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close, a move that could trigger selling by funds tracking the benchmarks. JPMorgan previously estimated that the exclusion could result in roughly $2.8 billion in selling pressure.

Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph that MSCI’s decision could help distinguish Bitcoin treasury companies from traditional operating businesses and limit indirect cryptocurrency exposure for passive investors.

“Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” he said.

Kirkley added that MSCI’s decision also raises broader questions about whether Bitcoin treasury companies should be classified alongside traditional operating businesses.

In its Aug. 31 response to MSCI’s proposed rules, Strategy argued that the changes were a pretext for targeting digital asset treasury companies. It also downplayed the potential financial impact, saying MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million of its shares, representing just 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding.

The stock’s decline coincided with a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $71,340 as of 4:08 p.m. ET on Thursday, down 4.3% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The total cryptocurrency market capitalization declined 3% to around $2.49 trillion.

#4995. Kalshi ends Donald Trump Jr. advisory role over Polymarket investment: Reuters

The prediction market operator said the decision was mutual and followed 1789 Capital’s investment in rival Polymarket, denying political considerations.

Prediction market platform Kalshi has ended its advisory relationship with Donald Trump Jr. after his venture capital firm increased its investment in rival Polymarket, Reuters reported Thursday.

A Kalshi spokesperson told Reuters that talks about ending Trump Jr.’s advisory role began in August, after Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, took the lead on Polymarket’s $1 billion funding round. The round would value the company at $21 billion, with 1789 Capital set to contribute about $300 million.

“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” the spokesperson said.

Trump Jr. joined Kalshi as a strategic adviser in January 2025 and received an equity stake reportedly worth $300,000 at the time, according to the Financial Times.

Kalshi’s spokesperson said political considerations played no role in the decision. Two people familiar with the matter told Reuters, however, that some within Kalshi had raised concerns about what Democrats’ midterm sweep of both chambers of Congress could mean for the company.
