#4994. Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Some Nvidia employees are calling on the company's board to bring back Jensen Huang, days after he resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital relationships, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired.

An internal "suggestion box" post, submitted by a longtime engineer prior to Huang's resignation, urged the board to take employee sentiment into account before acting, Wired reported. It has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, several of which asked the board to find a way to reinstate Huang. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," one anonymous commenter wrote.

The post also called on the board to share the findings of its investigation with staff and to formally seek their views on Huang continuing as CEO. One employee went further, sending a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit and declaring: "I stand by Jensen."

In the hours following Huang's departure, some two dozen Nvidia employees posted supportive messages on LinkedIn, while Wired said it could not find any employee posts backing his departure. The engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment, and Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to the outlet.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and a board member on Thursday, ending a 33-year tenure at the company he co-founded. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, and Jones, a former CEO of Synopsys, became the board's first chair. Nvidia did not give a reason for the resignation.

Huang told staff on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, without naming anyone.

The New York Times had reported in October that surveillance of Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, indicated that she had developed a "close relationship" with the Nvidia CEO. Per the Times, U.S. officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times reported that a U.S. memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied that she is a spy.

Alice Huang was CEO and chair of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and was investigated by Singapore police over possible false declarations relating to the company's server purchases, the country's Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday. She was not investigated for espionage, it said.

Police found insufficient evidence that she had committed any offenses, but concluded she had knowingly given them inaccurate information to downplay her role at Megaspeed, according to the ministry. She was issued a stern warning, left Singapore in February and was barred from returning. Investigations into Megaspeed and six other people are ongoing.

Alice Huang is now living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not yet concluded whether Huang was a spy, and that the FBI was investigating the reports, according to Reuters, which was unable to reach her for comment.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Jensen Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported directly to him. Powell has not commented.

On Thursday, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters, and Huang and a representative for the board did not respond. Huang has not commented on the reports since his Sunday email, according to Wired.

The calls inside Nvidia echo criticism of the board's decision from tech and crypto figures. Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao called it a mistake for Nvidia to let Huang resign, while Elon Musk said hiring him would be "an honor."

Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. Congressional committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview on December 1 and to testify at a Senate hearing on December 3, as lawmakers examine Nvidia's chip exports to China.

He and Nvidia also face a proposed shareholder class action over his alleged ties to Alice Huang.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under Kress.

#4992. NK hackers join memecoin trenches, xStocks adds Hong Kong equities: Asia Express

North Korean hackers launch memecoins to launder funds stolen in the Binance hack, while xStocks plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.

North Korean hackers created memecoins to launder cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to a report from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.Between Nov. 5 and 7, the hackers created at least six tokens on NEAR and used liquidity pools on decentralized exchanges to move $430,000 of stolen funds between wallets, Elliptic said. However, the tokens attracted almost no outside trading and were abandoned shortly after launch.

Elliptic said the same laundering technique was also used following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025, when North Korean-linked actors moved at least $24 million through a newly created token on the TRON blockchain.

Hong Kong’s wealthy investors are embracing crypto. (Chi Hung Wong)

Kraken parent Payward’s xStocks platform has added tokenized versions of more than 200 stocks listed in the United Kingdom and European Union.

Payward said the latest expansion brings xStocks’ offering to more than 1,500 tokenized assets. The company reported more than $45 billion in cumulative transaction volume and over 550,000 unique holders.

Payward said it plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.

Deputy Secretary for Financial Services Chan Ho-lim told FinTech Week the region will introduces a new licensing regime for virtual-asset trading, custody, advisory and management, via amendment bills that will be submitted to Legislative Council this year.

Police have arrested 22 people in a cross border money laundering investigation, that allegedly involved a over the counter crypto network that moved more than HKD$150 million (US$18 million) while attempting to obscure the origin of funds. Meanwhile, the US has sanctioned 41 entities allegedly linked to the Cambodia’s Prince Group, including a man named Qiu Yong, who is accused of running Hong Kong companies on behalf of the criminal organization.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) plans to allow crypto exchanges to suspend deposits and withdrawals when hacking is suspected, rather than waiting until a breach is confirmed.

The FSC said it would issue a no-action letter permitting preventive suspensions under certain conditions. Current rules prohibit exchanges from blocking withdrawals without legitimate grounds and explicitly allow restrictions only when a hacking incident is clearly established.

The regulator also called for round-the-clock monitoring and incident response, higher cold-wallet holdings, and stronger insurance coverage and reserves.

South Korean crypto exchange GOPAX announced on November 6 it was suspending trading, deposits and withdrawals and moving all user assets to cold wallets. The firm had received threatening emails that claimed a hack was imminent, and took the drastic step of putting everything on ice on the recommendation of financial authorities.

Japanese financial services giant Nomura Holdings is reportedly weighing a sale of its cryptocurrency subsidiary Laser Digital as Nomura’s European operations continue to post losses.

Nomura has held talks with potential buyers, including Marex Group but is yet to make a final decision and could keep the business.

Nomura’s European businesses posted a pretax loss of 7.4 billion yen ($46.5 million) in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, their fourth consecutive quarterly loss. The company posted pretax profits in every other reporting region over the same period.

Thailand is examining new rules for ETFs and ICO investors (Sasint)

Thailand’s securities regulator has proposed capping daily stablecoin deposits and withdrawals at 5 million baht ($148,000) each per customer at regulated crypto operators.

The limit would apply separately to deposits and withdrawals at each operator, Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said in a Thursday announcement. The regulator said the rules aim to curb money laundering, cybercrime and attempts to bypass cross-border money transfer rules.

The draft would bar stablecoin transfers to and from third-party wallets.

Thailand’s SEC will block access to Bitget from December 5. It has also proposed new tests for retail investors before allowing them to invest in ICOs. The tests would require knowledge of at least six areas including digital tokens and investor rights, blockchain technology, digital-asset wallets and distribution channels. The proposals will be up for comment until November 25. The SEC is also seeking feedback on new rules around margin loans and ETFs, but has ruled out allowing leveraged or crypto ETFs at this stage.

South Korean crypto firm Bithumb Asset, has invested $85 million into a luxury resort project in Hoi An in Vietnam being built by local real estate developer Asia Estate. Da Nang police have issued a warning about scams via “ghost” cryptocurrency projects that are really just ponzi schemes in disguise. They highlighted a fraud ring involving the DRK cryptocurrency project, led by Huynh Duc Van, 33, and seven accomplices, which was recently dealt with by law enforcement.

Nomura’s former head of crypto derivatives trading, John Kim, has joined Chicago-based DV Trading in Singapore to lead a new discretionary crypto-trading team. A Singapore woman lost S$78,000 (US$60,391) in a four-month long crypto scam after someone posing as an insurance buyer “helped” her to set up a crypto wallet. She initially believed she was making money, before getting cleared out after she was directed to the little known Qevorinex platform. International bank communication network Swift argued at Singapore FinTech Festival for shared standards to prevent digital assets from fragmenting across incompatible systems.

Morning Minute: Crypto Plummets as Jensen Huang Exits Nvidia

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

📉 Crypto Sells Off as Jensen Huang Exits Nvidia

Two weeks ago, The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s CEO had a close relationship with an executive at a Singapore chip buyer under US export-control investigation. Things escalated quickly from there.

On Sunday, Jensen Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years, and Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. On Wednesday, The Times reported a second relationship, this one with an executive who reports directly to him. Three Republican committee chairs were preparing a subpoena.

Thursday morning he resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The company gave no reason.

CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping the CFO job. She has been Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, through the entire AI buildout, and spent 13 years at Microsoft before that. The board also named Harvey Jones, formerly of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair, and started a search that will consider internal and external candidates with no timeline attached.

The stock fell as much as 14% before recovering to close down about 4%. Nvidia has now shed more than a trillion dollars in market value this month.

Bitcoin fell roughly 4% to a twelve-week low near $68,000, down from above $76,000 earlier in the week. ETH lost about 3% and is now below $2,000. Solana, BNB and XRP all fell between 3% and 5%. The broad market index was off about 4% on the day and 7% on the week.

It’s a bleak picture. But there are some local reasons for hope.

First, this is the exact price action that we mapped out in Wednesday’s newsletter, after analyzing the SPCX impact on Bitcoin and what similar price action for the Anthropic IPO would mean. TLDR - it mapped to a bottom on Nov 12 around the 200-week moving average (which hit last night).

Second, Binance reported Thursday afternoon that it has completed coverage of the assets affected by its $6.34 billion hack and published an expanded Proof of Reserves snapshot covering all 44 cryptocurrencies impacted. Many believe that the Binance post-hack aftermath has been weighing on crypto prices, and now perhaps this coverage will help alleviate some pain.

And then Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 results on Tuesday. Any positive news about Jensen succession planning, the Q3 results and/or future growth will likely stop the bleeding on one of the biggest assets across markets (also helping crypto most likely).

We will find out soon if it’s enough to stop the bleeding…

#4985. Maple Finance’s strategy rift sends co-founder, COO to the exits

Maple Finance co-founder Joe Flanagan and COO Ryan O’Shea are leaving over disagreements about the firm’s direction as SYRUP falls despite revenue growth.

Two senior executives are leaving onchain asset manager Maple Finance over disagreements about the firm’s direction as its SYRUP token slid more than 7% Thursday.

Maple co-founder and executive chairman Joe Flanagan said Wednesday he would leave after seven years at the firm, describing a growing divide with fellow co-founder and CEO Sidney Powell.

“Over time, our views on strategy, leadership, and life have moved further apart,” Flanagan wrote. “I believe Maple is best served by one co-founder leading it forward from here.”

Chief operating officer Ryan O’Shea also said in a Thursday post on X that he would leave after nearly five years at Maple. “I’ll be stepping down as COO. I’ve come to a different view on the direction Maple should take, and I’ve decided it’s time to step aside,” he wrote.

SYRUP traded at $0.12 at 10:36 p.m. UTC Thursday, down 7.5% over 24 hours and 12% over the past week, according to CoinGecko. The token had a market capitalization of about $145 million.

Maple and Powell did not respond to Cointelegraph’s requests for comment by publication.

In a statement published Wednesday, Maple confirmed that Flanagan was stepping down as chairman and leaving the company. “This is an agreed and orderly transition,” the company said, adding that his responsibilities would move to Powell and Maple’s existing leadership team.

The company did not announce a replacement chairman or specify how the departing executives’ duties would be carried out.

Flanagan said his differences with Powell reached a point where they were no longer constructive. “I am choosing to leave rather than continue supporting a direction I cannot stand behind,” he said. Flanagan added that he would help with the transition through the end of 2026.

O’Shea is stepping down effective Nov. 27. “I’ll have no ongoing role after that,” he wrote.

The departures come as Maple looks to expand beyond crypto-backed lending. In October, Powell said the firm planned to reach more customers through fintech partnerships and lend against a wider range of assets, including payments owed on loans made by fintech companies and securities backed by assets such as mortgages.

Related: Kraken, Maple launch onchain warehouse facility for crypto-backed institutional loans

The announcements come as Maple’s lending business continues to grow, while SYRUP is down 62% year to date and total value locked (TVL) has declined.

According to Token Terminal, Maple’s protocol revenue rose 8% year over year in October, while TVL fell around 11% between the end of September and Nov. 11.

Maple’s latest quarterly results also showed growth, with the company reporting $4.4 million in third-quarter revenue, up 5% from a year earlier. Assets under management rose 18% year over year to $4.7 billion.

Maple has also been using some of its revenue to buy back SYRUP tokens. In September, the company repurchased about 1.37 million tokens, twice as many as in August, according to its October update.

#4984. ‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

Charles Hoskinson said that the Cardano "roadmap is complete" and that everything he said would be built has finished. It came during a YouTube livestream Saturday where Hoskinson sparred with disgruntled investors as ADA sits down 94% from its 2021 high, per Decrypt data.

One viewer, named shevilkid1738, pushed Hoskinson's buttons by claiming he'd promised Cardano would overtake Bitcoin. The Cardano founder clapped back, saying there was no evidence he ever said that.

"I never promised that. I said I'd love for it to happen, and I believe that Cardano is a better store of value than Bitcoin is for a variety of reasons," Hoskinson said. "I don't promise price appreciation, or people overturning things. I say it's absolutely possible."

Shevilkid1738 responded over an hour later with a quote where Hoskinson said he "thinks" Cardano is "probably" going to become the biggest cryptocurrency in the world. Hoskinson highlighted the word think and said that he has "taken it as far as I can," explaining that the network is now decentralized and doesn't rely on him as a founder.

The viewer wasn't happy and called it "insane" for a founder to no longer have a responsibility to those who invested in their project.

"Under what conditions does that obligation end?" Hoskinson said, "The roadmap is complete. Everything I said is going to be built has been built. It reached four times the value of Honda. There's millions of people that have used it, and millions of people continue to use it. It is self-determining and self-governing, with its ability to pick and choose its own leaders without my consent."

Cardano’s roadmap was split into five eras: Byron, Shelly, Goguen, Basho, and Voltaire.

Byron launched the network in September 2017, Shelley added staking in July 2020, and Goguen brought smart contracts via the Alonzo hard fork in September 2021. Basho, the scaling era, came via the Vasil upgrade in September 2022, before the Chang hard fork kicked off Voltaire, the governance era, in September 2024.

The final piece to the puzzle occurred in January 2025, when the Plomin hard fork gave ADA holders "real voting power" over the blockchain’s future. This marked the transition to "full decentralized governance," and apparently the end of the final roadmap era.

"The goal was simple. There's a roadmap. Byron, Basho, Shelley, et cetera, et cetera, and it's done," Hoskinson said. "I have no power over this ecosystem."

Ultimately, though, Hoskinson says the issue that investors have is financial.

"You want me to pump your bags. That's what you're really saying. The job's not done till it's pumped," he said. "But guess what? It's never done then, because somebody comes in at $3 ADA, and then expects it to be five. And then somebody comes in at $5 ADA and expects it to be seven. If you retire at five, you've defrauded the person at five. If you retire at three, you've defrauded the person at three. There's no winning."

ADA hit an all-time high of $3.09 in 2021 and has been on a downward slide ever since. By 2023, it hit a low of $0.25 before pumping 384% to a high of $1.21 by the end of 2024. Since then, its price has tanked 86% to $0.17.

"Apparently, I have to go pump your bags, and if I don't, I'm a scammer," Hoskinson said. "Would you sign up for that deal? Would any human being sign up for that? I thought slavery was made illegal."

#4982. Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low

Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.

Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume.

Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023.

Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading.

Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total.

A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter.

Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.”

At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million.

Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere.

Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average.

Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3.

The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements.

Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday.

#4979. Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Britain's new crypto rules will still be in transition when global anti-money laundering assessors arrive next year, and the country will be judged on whether it can enforce against crypto laundering, a taskforce convened by the Royal United Services Institute has warned.

The report, published on Friday, sets out the issues the London-based defense and security think tank's taskforce expects to dominate the UK's 2027 evaluation by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The Paris-based body sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing, and its peer reviews, known as mutual evaluations, grade countries on whether their rules work in practice.

The UK's report is due to be agreed at FATF's February 2028 plenary. The taskforce, made up of experts from the private sector, law enforcement and civil society, met in September; its discussions are not attributed to individual members.

This will be the first UK evaluation in which FATF considers crypto, and the taskforce was clear that crypto is a "material risk" for the UK. The City of London Police assesses that 66% of investment fraud in the UK involves crypto, according to the report, while the UK's 2025 National Risk Assessment rated crypto money laundering high risk, up from medium in 2020.

The UK brought crypto firms under its money laundering rules in 2020, and legislation passed in February created a statutory crypto regime. The Financial Conduct Authority set out which crypto activities it will regulate in April and finalized its rulebook in June, but the mandatory regime does not take effect until October 25, 2027.

The taskforce doubted the UK would be able to show adequate implementation by the time FATF visits in June, and said the UK had moved more conservatively than Hong Kong, the EU and Singapore.

Members were unanimous that assessors would examine this, and pointed to over-the-counter brokers, which the National Crime Agency estimated in the 2025 risk assessment are likely to launder hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

The taskforce cited the Metropolitan Police's £5.5 billion (about $7.3 billion) crypto seizure, linked to a Chinese professional money launderer sentenced in 2025, as an encouraging sign of what the UK criminal justice system can do when it has the capacity. But one member said the success had not been repeated in enough cases, and that the UK had barely scratched the surface of crypto laundering. FATF is expected to test whether results match the risk rather than rest on one headline case, the report said.

It also warned that because the UK's regime, which resembles the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, focuses on identifiable crypto firms, it risks pushing the highest-risk crypto outside the FCA's perimeter. That would leave law enforcement to trace assets the regulator cannot reach, such as Tether's USDT, with the taskforce pointing to a July 2025 Treasury report that flagged the stablecoin as having been "extensively exploited" by Russian-speaking laundering networks. Members doubted law enforcement had been given the capability and resources to keep pace.

The taskforce did praise UK international cooperation, including Operation Destabilise, which targeted Russian-speaking networks converting street cash into crypto. But it flagged resourcing of the UK Financial Intelligence Unit and law enforcement's economic crime capacity as likely vulnerabilities.

FATF has been pressing countries on crypto enforcement more broadly. In July, it said nearly 93% of jurisdictions it surveyed had yet to apply its standards to qualifying DeFiplatforms.

#4976. The 16 Most Festive Cities in the US to Visit This Christmas Season

Even the most steadfast Scrooge will find themselves humming a holiday jingle in these places that pack on the seasonal cheer. The most festive cities in the US for Christmas are fully devoted to their merry-making, with multi-weekend celebrations, European-style holiday markets, millions of twinkling lights, and Christmas tree lighting ceremonies for the whole town to enjoy. Some tried and true classics appear on this list—the Big Apple, of course, is included—but others might come as a surprise. You’ll also find a city that celebrates the holidays in 18th-century style, a Danish town famous for its architecturally impressive gingerbread, and a ski destination that even sends Santa down the slopes. Below, tour the 15 most festive cities in the US for Christmas.

We couldn’t put together a Christmas list without giving a nod to NYC. The setting of many a holiday film, the Big Apple is full of Christmas spirit, including the Rockefeller Center tree lighting ceremony, Christmas shows like the Radio City Christmas Spectacular, the ice skating rinks in Central Park, and holiday windows at the iconic department stores.

Dog sledding, snowshoeing, skiing, and snowboarding are a major part of the holiday activities in this alpine city, which is home to the country’s largest lift-served ski resort, Park City Mountain. The resort’s Town Lift even carries Santa into Park City for an annual celebration with cocoa, carolers, and tunes. On Christmas Eve, Santa returns for a torchlight parade as over 100 ski and snowboard instructors carve their way down the mountain.

Can’t make it to Copenhagen before Christmas? Instead, head to Solvang—a deeply Danish town only about 35 miles from Santa Barbara that puts a Scandinavian spin on holiday cheer. The city’s seasonal celebration is called Julefest, which takes place from late November through early January and features holiday markets, a parade, carolers, and holiday concerts. Be sure to swing by The Solvang Bakery, famous for its elaborate gingerbread houses.

If you’re dreaming of a white Christmas, you’re pretty much guaranteed to see some snow in Vail, where alpine sports are in full swing by December. In addition to hitting the slopes at Vail Ski Resort, wandering its idyllic village—with cobblestone walkways, Bavarian-style architecture, and tons of twinkling lights—will make you feel like you’re in a real-life storybook. Take part in an ugly sweater fun run, do some holiday shopping at Kris Kringle Market, and take in a free skating show, featuring world-class athletes.

This tinsel-loving town in southern Indiana, about 60 miles from Louisville, Kentucky, celebrates Christmas year round. Holiday World, an amusement park with rides named after Santa’s reindeer; Santa’s Candy Castle, a confectionary shop that dates back to 1935; and the Santa Claus Christmas Store, stocked with 8,000 ornaments, are open beyond just December. But the last month of the year is when the holiday vibes kick into high gear. Over the first three weekends of December, the town hosts its annual Santa Claus Christmas Celebration, including a Christmas parade, an arts and crafts show, and elaborate holiday light displays. The city is also home to the Santa Claus Museum & Village, where local “elves” answer letters to Santa for kids from all over.

Despite its warm temperatures and palm trees instead of pines, Charleston curates a ridiculously cozy holiday scene. One beloved tradition is the Holiday Festival of Lights at James Island County Park, which includes a spectacle of more than 750 illuminated displays (even the palm trees are aglow), a holiday train ride, and visits with Santa. Elsewhere, historic homes are decked in vintage decor, and residential neighborhoods like I’On—just 15 minutes from downtown—go all in, with luminary-lined sidewalks, horse-drawn carriages, and neighbors gathering at the European-inspired wine bar Saint Urban’s for post-caroling sips.

The Windy City embraces the holidays with travel-worthy Christmas markets. The most famous is Christkindlmarket, a European-style outdoor extravaganza with handcrafted gifts, mulled wine, and giant German pretzels. On Michigan Avenue, an illuminated nighttime parade, The Wintrust Magnificent Mile Lights Festival, kicks off the season; an ice skating rink opens in Millennium Park; and hotels deck their halls in elaborately festive fashion. For example, The Pendry Chicago transforms its rooftop bar, Château Carbide, into a winter wonderland with cozy chalets, each featuring a personal fireplace.

Take a trip back in time at Colonial Williamsburg, which celebrates Christmas with 18th-century flair. While in town, make sure to visit the Busch Gardens Christmas Town, decorated with eight million lights.

Asheville’s iconic Biltmore Estate, built by George Vanderbilt, is America’s largest home. How fitting, then, that it features one of the grandest Christmas displays in the country. More than 70 trees fill the 175,000-square-foot house for the holiday season. In 2023, Hallmark even premiered a fantasy rom-com inspired by the spectacular, appropriately titled A Biltmore Christmas.

Experience an Ozark Mountain Christmas in Branson, the Live Music Show Capital of the World. (There are, of course, many special performances throughout the season.) Stroll down the two-and-a-half-mile Shepherd of the Hills Trail of Lights, or see the five million Christmas lights and 1,000 decorated trees at Silver Dollar City.

Starting December 20, this town hosts the 12 Days of Aspen, during which local businesses offer holiday activities to visitors and residents, from designing your own gift wrap at the St. Regis to a performance of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol at the Wheeler Opera House.

From November to January, visit the Gilded Age mansions in Newport to see them filled with Christmas decorations. Plus, the whole town partakes in Christmas in Newport, a monthlong holiday celebration established in 1971, where residents and businesses alike decorate and host events.

The crown jewel of the Jersey Shore, this seaside town is filled with quaint bed and breakfasts and charming shops. The Victorian houses that line its streets are decorated with wreaths, lights, and garlands—take a ride on a holiday-themed trolley or join a popular walking tour to see them all.

Who says you need to have snow for Christmas? In Newport Beach, you can enjoy a 108-year-old tradition: the Newport Beach Christmas Boat Parade. More than a million people watch yachts, boats, and kayaks sail through the harbor each year. Outside of the annual spectacular, the parks services helps further set the holiday tone, adding Christmas trees in unexpected places, like at the Crystal Cove State Park, seen here.

Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, hours after he resigned as CEO.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second company employee, Reuters reported, bringing the number of alleged extramarital affairs to three.

The report, citing two people familiar with the matter, followed Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and a board member on Thursday. Reuters did not identify the other employee in its report and said attempts to reach her were unsuccessful.

#4971. Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks

The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC.

US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation.

The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission.

The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks.

Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill

Levine, a Republican, was nominated for an SEC term ending June 5, 2030, replacing Peirce, who left the agency in October. Peirce was a leading advocate for clearer crypto rules at the SEC, helping shape its approach to digital assets as the former head of its Crypto Task Force, while Levine’s views on crypto regulation are less publicly established.

Trump also nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, for the SEC seat held by Caroline Crenshaw, whose term has also expired. Johnson’s proposed term ends June 5, 2029. Johnson has advocated for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules for crypto firms in her time at the CFTC.

For the CFTC, Trump nominated Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland, both of whom worked on the Clarity Act. CFTC Chairman Mike Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” for CFTC commissioners and said he looked forward to working with them upon their confirmation.

The nominees would typically appear before the Senate Banking Committee for the SEC positions and the Senate Agriculture Committee for the CFTC roles. Following committee consideration, their nominations would go to the full Senate, where confirmation requires a majority vote.

#4967. Reformation’s Debut Home Collection Gives French Rugs an LA Attitude

For years, people shopping at Reformation have asked about something the brand didn’t sell. “One of the biggest comments that we get is that the stores look so beautiful and the rugs are amazing,” says Lauren Caris Cohan, the brand’s chief creative officer. Typically, she says, one question follows that observation: “Where can we get them?” Until now, the answer was nowhere; Thomas Coccimiglio, founder of the French rugmaker Les Editions de Tapis, is “really precious” about his designs for Reformation stores, Cohan says, and doesn’t reuse them for other clients.

Today, Reformation’s collaboration with Les Editions de Tapis makes the coveted rugs available to the public, with nine limited-edition styles, all made to order and priced between $1,000 and $5,000.

Long before he began outfitting Reformation showrooms, Coccimiglio spent more than 15 years as a textile designer in fashion, working in London, Paris, and New York. At Tory Burch, his trips to meet embroiderers in Italy and India eventually led him to rug-making, and during the pandemic, he left fashion for interiors, though his fashion background continues to influence him, even in the way he speaks about rugs: “I approach a rug almost as I would a piece of embroidery on a garment.”

Reformation opens more than 15 stores a year, Cohan says, and each one gets its own hand-sketched motif and custom colorway from Coccimiglio. “There’s a bit of a French sense of humor, a bone-dry sense of humor, in our [Reformation] brand DNA,” Cohan says, “that’s reflected in Thomas’ designs.”

For the new capsule collection of rugs, Reformation gave Coccimiglio full creative direction. The conversations that launched the collaboration involved Marie Antoinette, swans, a lot of pink and blue—all components also reflected in the partnering 12-piece clothing campaign, live today. To help inspire a cohesive thread linking Coccimiglio’s line to the ethos of the brand, he also revisited years of store designs for details to incorporate. “There’s something nostalgic about these pieces, almost like a little Proustian madeleine,” Coccimiglio says. “For customers who have experienced Reformation's stores over the years, these pieces might feel strangely familiar, almost iconic.”

The Chintz rugs set two crossed palm trees (Cohan’s idea, which Coccimiglio sketched by hand) between trailing vine borders, with herons and swans tucked at their roots. Swans Fans puts two black-outlined swans among spiky fan palms on a French blue foundation. Le Chat leaves a field of lilac almost entirely empty, save for one striped cat walking a broken black line. Le Classique has an ivory ground, two wavering oxblood borders, and a single dot, fitting anyone with French sensibilities sans menagerie.

The rugs are hand-knotted from wool, silk, and linen. Coccimiglio manufactures his larger pieces in India, where he finds the wool softer and better suited to big formats. Smaller editions come from Nepal, where Himalayan wool is denser, and the results are ornate, “like jewelry,” says Coccimiglio. While you could find a less expensive rug elsewhere, Cohan points out that Coccimiglio’s are designed for longevity of use—plus, the rugmaker’s own work outside the Reformation collaboration costs considerably more. “This is a much more accessible price point for something so detailed and so custom,” she says.

Cohan, who restores midcentury houses in Los Angeles with her husband Matt Jacoby under the name Bob Audrey, doesn’t picture a single kind of room to house these rugs. “You could have it in a midcentury house in the Hollywood Hills, but it also would look so stunning in [a] herringbone-floor apartment in New York City,” she says.

The campaign was shot in a house at the top of Wonderland Park in Laurel Canyon, a 1950s enclave of single-story midcentury houses that includes Pierre Koenig’s Case Study House No. 21. Coccimiglio, meanwhile, works from a 17th-century hôtel particulier in Dijon. It’s fitting that the premise of the collection enmeshes old-world France with modern LA, as Coccimiglio places his work “somewhere between these two worlds: French heritage and contemporary culture.”

The collection is available to shop on Reformation.com on Nov. 9.

#4965. Bitcoin slides below $70K amid thin liquidity, ETF outflows

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 as crypto sentiment hit its lowest level in more than four months, with analysts warning of institutional outflows, thinning liquidity and elevated leverage.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, extending its recent decline as investor sentiment deteriorated amid institutional outflows, tightening liquidity and broader macroeconomic pressures.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading at $68,607.23 at the time of writing, down 9.2% in the last week, according to CoinGecko.

The decline coincided with a sharp decline in market sentiment. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell to 20 on Friday, its lowest reading in more than four months, putting it in “extreme fear.” The index last reached that level on July 8.

Bitcoin’s seven-day price chart. Source: CoinGecko

Vikram Subburaj, CEO of crypto exchange Giottus, attributed Bitcoin’s weakness to institutional outflows, tightening crypto liquidity and expectations of a December Federal Reserve interest rate hike. “Investors should avoid chasing short-term dips or using excessive leverage,” he said.

In a Friday report, 10x Research highlighted Bitcoin’s divergence from US equities. Between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12, Bitcoin declined 5.9% while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, suggesting the cryptocurrency was responding more to rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar than to technology stocks.

The research firm said Bitcoin was increasingly trading alongside gold, which fell 5.5% over the same period, as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.

Meanwhile, institutional trading platform Talos also warned that thin liquidity and elevated leverage could amplify market volatility. Its weekly report showed Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

“Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos. “A rebuild in order-book depth and a turn in capital flows would provide a firmer foundation for recovery.”

The selloff follows sustained withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows across nine consecutive trading sessions through Wednesday, while broader funds shed nearly $1.44 billion over five sessions.

Preliminary Farside Investors data showed another $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, although figures for BlackRock and Fidelity were still pending.

#4961. Microsoft 365 outage hits Outlook email and Teams calendars worldwide

Microsoft began a wider patch rollout Friday as the outage disrupted government email and Microsoft 365 connectors in ChatGPT and Claude.

A global Microsoft 365 outage continued into Friday, disrupting Outlook email and some Teams features.

Microsoft said in a 7:25 am UTC update that a patch had improved stability on some servers and that it was working to deploy the fix more widely. The update, republished by the University of Pennsylvania, gave no timetable for restoration.

The outage began Thursday, leaving some users unable to access their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft said a process that handles secure connection became overloaded, causing affected servers to stop processing requests.

The company said it attempted to restore services by restarting infrastructure, redirecting network traffic and expanding server capacity. Microsoft said there was no indication of a security breach.

The outage also affected features in Microsoft Copilot and Defender for Office 365. In Teams, users had trouble scheduling meetings and sending invitations. Microsoft said most Teams calls and chats continued to work.

Businesses and government agencies worldwide use Microsoft 365 for email and scheduling. Microsoft reported more than 450 million paid commercial seats for the suite in an October filing. Exchange Online hosts the mailboxes and calendars those organizations use, and outside apps, including AI assistants, rely on the same service to retrieve that data when users connect their work accounts.

OpenAI reported errors in ChatGPT’s Microsoft 365 connector. Anthropic said the outage caused most email, calendar and search requests through Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector to fail.

The US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit said its clerk’s office could neither send nor receive email for much of Thursday. Japan’s Finance Ministry said it was unable to receive email on Friday and Singapore’s Government Technology Agency told CNA that government email was among systems affected.

#4960. The Guy’s Guide to Adult Acne

We’re all stressed AF. The food we’re eating probably isn’t helping. Everyone told us we wouldn’t have to worry about our hormones going crazy after our teen years. What the heck is going on?

THE YEAR WAS 1997. I’d just made the varsity baseball team as a freshman, and I was ready to shoot my shot with every senior girl who’d give me the time of day. The only problem: I had also hard-launched my pepperoni face. I’m not talking surface-level New York slice stuff—these breakouts were Detroit-style-pizza deep. Every clogged pore had clocked in at the same time, and I was an absolute wreck.

For six months, I’d burned through everything the CVS aisles had to offer: Oxy Pads, Stridex, Noxzema, whatever stuff was hawking a promise of clear skin. Nothing worked. My face just got redder, drier, and more irritated. My mom (thank god for her) dragged me to the dermatologist, and I walked out with a prescription for isotretinoin, a.k.a. Accutane. Five months later, my skin was completely clear. My mini CVS stash went into the trash, and I thought that’d be the end of it.

I was wrong. I spent years assuming that because I took Accutane as a teenager, I’d paid my dues, but as a 44-year-old dude, I still get the occasional pimple or two—seemingly right before a big work meeting or whenever I have a lot of stuff on my plate. And it still messes with my head. Does my hygiene suck? Are my hormones to blame? Am I sweating too much? Apparently, I’m not the only one.

According to Christopher Bunick, MD, PhD, an associate professor of dermatology at the Yale School of Medicine, 83 percent of teen boys will deal with acne before they reach their 20s, which is often due to a surge in testosterone at the time. And while acne typically clears up as testosterone levels stabilize in our 20s, it can make a surprise comeback in our 30s, 40s, 50s, and beyond—with around 20 percent of men in their 30s dealing with breakouts, but only 12 percent seeking treatment from a medical professional. It’s not just a skin issue: Research shows that adult acne is consistently linked to a higher risk of developing anxiety, depression, and reduced self-esteem.

Acne (not to be mistaken for folliculitis, which can result from shaving) is mainly caused by a combination of excess oil production and dead skin cells that clog pores. This can create an environment where strains of Cutibacterium acnes—the bacteria naturally found on your skin—become imbalanced and trigger inflammation. This could look like blackheads and whiteheads, raised pustules and papules, or the deeper, more painful nodules or cysts that are more likely to scar. And despite what your instincts tell you, excessively scrubbing your face won’t help—it could actually harm your skin barrier. “You cannot wash away hormones,” says Dr. Bunick. Acne is an inflammatory condition, not a hygiene problem.

Scientists still aren’t sure exactly what makes some guys more susceptible to acne than others, but genetics and hormones are two leading factors. Research suggests about 80 percent of your acne risk is inherited. Your genes determine how sensitive your skin is to the hormones (i.e., androgens) that regulate the sebaceous glands and how aggressively your immune system overreacts to fight the inflammation. Then there are the lifestyle factors that play a smaller role but can collectively add up, such as diet (Dr. Bunick is a believer in the gut-skin axis—the idea that an imbalanced gut microbiome can drive systemic inflammation that can predispose you to acne), stress (this spikes cortisol, which also drives oil production and contributes to inflammation), sleep deprivation (same), and testosterone replacement therapy.

Though there isn’t a cure for acne yet, there are plenty of treatment options. “Untreated acne doesn’t just affect your skin. It affects how you move through the world,” says Dr. Bunick. “Acne impacts confidence, whether it’s making friends, having a social or dating life, or performance in work, sports, or other extracurriculars.” Earlier intervention means less of a psychosocial toll, less scarring, and (you heard the man) more confidence.

So if your bathroom still looks like mine did in the ’90s, it’s time to investigate what might be causing the chaos in your largest organ and learn how to treat it. The stories below will help you get your skin clear and, hopefully, keep it that way.

Bob Gearing is a New York-based writer covering men’s grooming from the perspective of a very real (and very sweaty) dude. By day, he’s a well-SPF’d tech sales bro; by night, he’s a red-light mask guy who definitely didn’t think he’d care this much about skincare. When he’s not testing the latest face serum, you’ll find him sweating through a round of golf or holding out hope that the Lions will make the Super Bowl before he dies.

#4957. Jane Street boosts Fidelity Bitcoin ETF holdings nearly 8x, trims IBIT

Jane Street ended Q3 with 19% fewer shares in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF, and a higher share price lifted the stake’s value to $957 million.

Jane Street’s share count in Fidelity’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) rose nearly eightfold in the third quarter, while its holdings in BlackRock’s fund fell 19%.

The trading giant ended September with 7.01 million shares of Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC0, up from about 887,000 at the end of June. The position was worth $509 million on Sept. 30, according to its second-quarter and third-quarter filings.

Jane Street’s holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) fell to 20.22 million shares from 24.88 million. A higher share price lifted the reported value of its stake to $957 million from $828 million.

Jane Street was the largest reported institutional holder of BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF at the end of June after boosting its share count by 324% in Q2, according to 13F Pro. IBIT is the world’s largest spot Bitcoin ETF with $56 billion in net assets as of Thursday.

The firm also added nearly 9 million shares (about $249 million) of the ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB), while more than doubling its holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA) by 7.83 million shares (about $158 million).

JPMorgan Chase increased its IBIT holdings by 9.6% in the third quarter, adding about 1 million shares to reach 11.41 million. The US banking giant’s reported IBIT position rose to around $540 million.

In contrast, JPMorgan nearly erased its direct holdings in BlackRock’s ETHA, reducing its position from 1.17 million shares at the end of June to just 399 shares.

Related: Barclays boosts BlackRock’s IBIT stake 48% ahead of key Q3 13F filings

The bank also increased its holdings in Bitcoin treasury company Strategy by 36% to nearly 849,000 shares, worth about $131 million at the end of Q3.

Laurore, which lists a Hong Kong business address in its SEC filing, reduced its IBIT holdings by 33%, cutting its position by 1.6 million shares to 3.25 million, worth about $154 million by the end of Q3. Laurore drew attention in February 2026 after disclosing an IBIT position worth $436 million at the end of 2025.

#4956. How a Society Photographer Fell in Love With an Unexpected Upstate Victorian Home

I had no intention of buying the house on Willard Place. I only added it to the short list of Hudson properties I planned to visit out of sheer morbid curiosity. The house looked completely crazy online, with its wild colors and eccentric embellishments, inside and out—a confounding mix of hideous and fabulous. I felt compelled to check it out in person. Real estate agent extraordinaire Julia Crowley made the appointment at Willard the first stop on our house-hunting itinerary. The artist Helen Marden, a dear friend and owner of the nearby Hotel Tivoli, decided to come along for the ride. “What are we doing here?” she asked when we got out of the car. I’d forgotten to mention this purely voyeuristic side trip.

The polychrome exterior of Craig-Martin's house in Hudson, New York.

Craig-Martin on the front steps of her home with her beloved Roo, a whippet and chihuahua mix.

Above the mantel hangs a painting by Haitian artist Ramphis Magloire. To the left is an etching by Brice Marden, a gift from the artist to Craig-Martin’s son on the occasion of his birth. To the right is a Fernand Léger print, a gift from the homeowner’s artist father, Michael Craig-Martin. A mix of Indian, Moroccan, Italian, Chinese, and Indonesian art and furnishings testifies to a well-traveled life.

I was fully expecting the polychrome Victorian house to be crammed full of furniture, as seen in the online listing. But when Helen, Julia, and I stepped in, it was breathtakingly empty, save for shafts of winter sunlight that illuminated the generous rooms and old wood floors. It became clear that the grotesque furniture I’d seen in the photos was virtual—a terrifying misuse of AI. We sat on the old iron radiators, quietly absorbing the beautiful proportions and unexpected calm. It was fabulous—that was undeniable—but with five bedrooms, it was far more house than I was looking for, and seemed daunting for one person. Helen disagreed. At the next stop, she took one look at the house from the car and didn’t bother to get out.

Craig-Martin seated on a chaise on the terrace off the dining room. A painting by Joe Brainard hangs above a vase from Regan & Smith in Hudson, New York.

George Nakashima chairs surround a table from India made of dismantled boat parts.

An Indonesian stool sits beside a rattan chaise beneath an Indian elephant mobile on the terrace.

A barracuda sculpture by Dalwa Donoffre rests on an Aalto stool in the window bay of the dining room. Beside it, an Ashley Bickerton sculpture sits on a marble pedestal from Rajasthan, surrounded by Stone Age tools, a whale vertebra, and a turquoise bowl by Mary Heilmann.

In the entry hall, a Josef Albers print is installed above a rustic table with a Cameroonian fertility figure.

Over the following months I continued looking in the area, but nothing struck a chord. “You should be thinking about Willard,” Helen kept saying. “It’s a good house.” Completed in 1875, the classic Victorian was built during the whaling boom that enriched Hudson and dotted the town with other equally eccentric Victorian homes replete with multiple bow windows, terraces, and turrets. It had been standing empty and neglected for years, but a thorough assessment did not threaten any looming “old house” disasters. Unable to get the beauty of the place out of my mind, I made an offer.

An ant sculpture from Deyrolle in Paris joins an array of copper pans in the kitchen.

A pastel drawing by Finbar Craig-Martin hangs above a Chinese console table with bagel sculptures by Hanna Liden.

I enlisted a friend to help me move in, though furniture would have to come later. We drove up from the city in a rented van filled with Moroccan rugs and two inflatable mattresses, and ate pizza on the floor in front of a roaring fire. Two years later, I can’t imagine living without the house’s spaciousness and light, or its grand old-world flourishes. Frankly, I don’t know how I coped for so many years without a Norma Desmond staircase. It seems unrealistic now to imagine life without one, which confirms my suspicion that luxury is a one-way trip.

Artworks in the primary bedroom include (clockwise from far left) a painting by Michael Craig-Martin, a painting by Charlie Lucas (above mantel), a light sculpture by Theo Rosenblum (on mantel), a Jessica Craig-Martin photograph of Fran Lebowitz (floor), and a round painting on glass by Finbar Craig-Martin.

A crayon drawing of the homeowner at age two by her mother, Jan Hashey, sits on a Balinese child’s chair in the bathroom.

Jessica Craig-Martin in the bedroom of her son, Finbar. To the right of a movie poster from Ghana is a photograph by Jason Noyes.

Craig-Martin’s son’s room has a Paul McCobb desk, an Eames chair modified by artists Eric Wesley and Piero Golia. and a poster of Ursula Andress from the movie Dr. No above a rustic kitchen cabinet.

In Finbar’s room, a Nate Lowman pizza painting hangs beside a foam-core cutout of David Bowie.

I added a red refrigerator and stove to match the kitchen’s vintage red Formica countertops, and a lifetime’s worth of art and ephemera, from artwork by my parents and friends to artifacts, textiles, and natural oddities collected on various travels. There are unnatural oddities, too. For example, I have a weakness for cheap Japanese plushy cushions, my favorite being a huge pink peach that, when viewed from a certain angle, morphs unmistakably into a huge pink ass. It is also evident that I favor crocodiles and alligators in any form, though if you asked me why, I couldn’t say. One thing is certain: We are a very long way from “form follows function.” Fortunately, at least to my eye, the house absorbed my proclivity for both the ridiculous and the sublime with grace. Helen was right. It is a good house, and it has welcomed me, perhaps recognizing in me a madness that in some way matches its own.

The home office/library features an Alvar Aalto chair and stool, a low alligator table Craig-Martin found on the street in New York City, and a totem from the Solomon Islands displayed beside the fireplace. On the mantel, a Michael Craig-Martin hammer sculpture is surmounted by a Brice Marden etching. A tower of Hermès boxes holds a corner of the room.

Detail of the Hermès box tower. Behind it is an etching by Joel Shapiro, a gift from the artist.

Exterior view of Willard House and its eccentric, polychromatic Victorian façade.

Jessica Craig-Martin’s memoir, I Regret I Am Able to Attend, publishes November 10, 2026.

#4953. The Paths to Clear(er) Skin

With a little trust and patience, it’s possible to find a solution that works for you. These three guys are proof.

Treating adult acne can feel like one big science experiment—until now. This is the guy’s guide to adult acne. Read the rest of the stories here.

IT’S ONE THING to get advice from a doctor (still important and invaluable), but it’s another to hear from other guys who’ve been there. Guys who understand what it’s like to cancel plans because of a whopper of a zit. Guys who’ve also hesitated to take their shirts off at the pool for fear of being judged for their bacne. We wanted to hear about their struggles, and successes—what finally worked to help them send breakouts packing and regain their confidence. As you’ll learn from these three men, no two plans are the same. But with a little consistency and some experimentation, blemish-free skin is possible.

I like to take care of myself. I work out at least five times a week. I’m consistent with my diet. But my confidence takes a hit because of my acne. Since I was a teenager, I’ve dealt with deep cystic breakouts that have totally upended my life. I’ve canceled dates; I’ve canceled trips; I won’t leave the house when I have a flare. It’s improved as I’ve gotten older—since 2023 I’ve been using Winlevi, a prescription hormone-blocking cream, in the morning and at night, and Tazorac, a doctor-dispensed retinoid that I’ve been using since my 20s, at night—but I still deal with the occasional breakout. And it still messes with my confidence.

I went to Greece over the summer, and I could feel a big one coming under my skin. The one thing that really makes a difference is the La Roche-Posay Effaclar Duo+M treatment, which you can get for $25 at the drugstore. I apply it religiously every few hours as soon as I feel a zit coming on, and sometimes it helps it come to a head faster or stops it from forming altogether. I’ve found a routine that works, but acne is always something lingering in the back of my mind. —Derek Monacchio, 38, tax director

Back acne is something I’ve had my entire life, but honestly, I just thought it was something I’d always have to deal with. I couldn’t reach back there with a cream or a wash, and I didn’t want to go on Accutane or any prescription medications. Even though most people couldn’t see it, I’d get very self-conscious whenever I’d take my shirt off in public, which sucked because I take good care of my body.

That all changed when I went in for a laser hair removal appointment at a physician-led laser center, The Kaga Institute, about six months ago. The office staff knew my situation with the breakouts on my back and told me they had something that could help—a new laser called AviClear, which supposedly suppresses oil gland production. I was curious, so I gave it a try. After three sessions, the pimples on my back were gone. It was totally painless for me—especially when compared to the laser hair removal I’ve tried. Each click of the laser felt like a warm sensation for a millisecond, and I was able to continue with my laser hair removal at the same time. Now that I’ve finished my series of treatments, I was told the results should improve with time. It feels great to have found a solution that works. I’m ready for next summer already. —William Sebok, 42, construction company owner

There’s a perception that when you have acne, you find a solution and then it’s over. That has not been my experience. My first breakouts (a mix of whiteheads and inflamed red bumps) started just as I was hitting puberty, around age 11, and persisted well into my 30s. I’ve seen a few different dermatologists since I was 15 and was prescribed everything under the sun—from clindamycin (a prescription antibiotic) to Accutane. I would take the medications for a few months at a time, and some would help for a while, but once I stopped, my skin would inevitably break out again. Plus, I experienced some side effects from the Accutane, including significant lethargy.

After I stopped taking the medications, I started looking at the labels of the skin care products I was using and noticed that when the ingredient list was extremely long, there was a higher likelihood there would be something in there that would clog my pores. [Editor’s note: Look for the label “noncomedogenic,” a.k.a. not pore clogging, on your products.] For me, it became more about avoiding certain products and soothing the skin barrier. I also became much more careful about not overloading my routine with too many strong ingredients. I focused instead on making sure the products I was using were appropriate for my acne-prone skin. That was the game changer. Another thing that causes my skin to react is my diet. If I’m eating a lot of high-glycemic foods and meals that are high in sugar, I immediately break out. I also try to wash my face or shower immediately after every workout, and if I can’t, I spray on a hypochlorous acid spray to kill the bacteria. Less is more, and I’m proof of that. —Brute Choi, 37, content creator

Brian Underwood is beauty director at Women’s Health, where he oversees content strategy for the brand across all platforms, including digital, print, and social. Underwood previously served as beauty and wellness director at Oprah Daily and O, The Oprah Magazine. #4952. DOJ moves to seize $1.2B from Binance hack, disrupts FaceStealer scam

Authorities froze over $2.7 billion in Binance hack proceeds, while the separate FaceStealer scam stole over $400 million in 18 months.

The US Department of Justice said Thursday it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance.

The authorization covers part of the more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets that US authorities and private-sector partners have frozen since the Oct. 29 hack. Investigators are still working to recover additional funds, the department said in its announcement.

The FBI attributed the Binance hack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group in a cyber alert. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement.

Binance said it had covered the affected assets with its own funds and that a new proof-of-reserves snapshot showed at least one-to-one backing for customer assets, according to its Thursday post on X.

In November 2025, the DOJ announced a separate enforcement action targeting about $15 million in cryptocurrency linked to North Korean hackers known as APT38.

Related: Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

In a separate case, US authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in FaceStealer, a North Korean social engineering campaign that stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months, the DOJ said.

The hackers used secretly recorded footage of previous victims and AI-generated deepfakes of prominent crypto figures to gain targets’ trust on video calls. They used bogus technical fixes to trick targets into installing malware, the DOJ said.

The campaign targeted people working in crypto and Web3. The hackers also increasingly targeted open-source software developers and maintainers in attempts to gain access to their devices and software repository accounts.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. The bureau also published guidance on how to protect against the scheme and what to do after a compromise in a public advisory.

Redacted stills from webcam videos recorded by FaceStealer hackers. Source: FBI

The DOJ said the hackers behind FaceStealer are known publicly by several names, including Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, APT38, BlueNoroff and Stardust Chollima.

#4947. Bitcoin returns to 200-week trend line as analyst sees risk of $57.7K next

Bitcoin price action interacted with its 200-week simple moving average for the first time since mid-August as it fell below $68,000.

Bitcoin (BTC) fell to $67,500 on Friday, slipping below its 200-week simple moving average on its first test of the level in nearly three months.

TradingView data showed that Bitcoin last touched its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) on Aug. 19.

BTC/USD one-day chart with the 200-week SMA. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The 200-week SMA has served as a reference point for Bitcoin’s cycle lows, acting as support or resistance during bear markets. Bitcoin traded around the average from March to October 2023 and again from June to mid-August this year. Decisive moves back above it on the weekly chart have preceded sharper rallies.

In his latest analysis, Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, flagged the 200-week SMA as having confluence with a resistance/support flip level on Bitcoin’s relative strength index (RSI).

Weekly RSI has returned to 41.5, a level that it established as support in late July after it spent several weeks attempting a breakout.

“Losing 41.5 on Weekly RSI opens the door to test the cycle low at $57.7k,” Alan wrote Friday on X, noting the bullish implications that successfully defending the support zone would have.

BTC/USD one-week chart with 200 SMA; RSI data. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

BTC price downside accelerated on Friday as Asia markets reacted to the resignation and ongoing controversy around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng finished the day down 1.55%, while South Korea’s KOSPI Composite Index ended 0.98% lower.

Related: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, exits board; shares plunge

US stock-market futures fell slightly, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 0.2% as analysis eyed a redistribution of capital into Nvidia’s competitors, preserving the AI trade.

Nasdaq 100 futures one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

“What you’re seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up,” said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at asset manager Manulife Investment Management, told CNBC.

Nvidia stock was 0.7% higher pre-market, meanwhile, amid reports of growing support for Huang’s return. An internal post quoted by Wired drew more than 1,600 comments from employees.

#4942. The 17 Most Beautiful Ski Resorts to Visit This Winter—Including Three in the US

When winter arrives, the world’s most idyllic mountain towns transform into playgrounds for serious adrenaline seekers. But, as the most beautiful ski resorts prove, the appeal of an extraordinary alpine escape extends well beyond its slopes. Why kick off your ski boots just anywhere when you could do so in a castle-like hotel in the Swiss Alps or a secluded Japanese ryokan tucked among snow-covered forests? Sure, the world-renowned runs are worth traveling for, but sometimes so are the ski hotels themselves. Think Michelin-starred restaurants, award-winning spas, art-filled interiors, and architecture that makes the most of its dramatic surroundings. Here, AD rounds up 17 of the most beautiful ski resorts to visit this winter, whether you’re an alpine ace, a beginner ski bum, or purely an après enthusiast.

Getting to Zaborin Ryokan is an adventure in itself, which means you know it’ll be good. After landing at New Chitose Airport in Sapporo, it’s a two-hour drive to the ryokan, which is hidden in the Hanazono woods of Hokkaido. Arriving at the property feels like discovering some sort of secretive lair from a Bond flick—a series of low-lying villas covered in snow suddenly reveal themselves. Built on natural hot springs, each of the villas has its own indoor and outdoor onsen, plus floor-to-ceiling windows and a private balcony with views of Mount Yōtei, the area’s dormant volcano, in the distance. Make an appointment with the in-house matcha master and prepare your taste buds for a multicourse Japanese kaiseki meal. If you can tear yourself away from your absurdly serene suite long enough to ski or snowboard, the ryokan will arrange your transfer to and from Hanazono Niseko ski area, just seven minutes away by car.

Modernist design meets mountainside adventure at Pendry Park City, a ski-in, ski-out luxury resort where “hitting the slopes” means basically just stepping outside. Tucked in Canyons Village at Park City Mountain—the largest ski resort in the US, with over 7,000 skiable acres spread across two connected mountains—this slopeside sanctuary is right next to the brand-new, high-speed Sunrise Gondola. After a day appreciating the powder, guests gather at Après Pendry for fondue and crème brulée espresso martinis either by the fire or outside. Alternatively, they head up to the rooftop for a dip in the year-round heated pool and hot tub, plus immaculate mountain views.

Located in St. Moritz, Switzerland, the Carlton Hotel boasts 60 luxurious suites that blend old-world grandeur with contemporary elements. The resort is also home to the Michelin-starred restaurant Da Vittorio.

The Gstaad Palace in Switzerland opened in 1913 and has catered to jet-setters and stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and Marlene Dietrich throughout its long history. The castlelike hotel overlooks the streets of Gstaad, which are filled with high-end boutiques.

The Pines Lodge, a RockResort is a rustic Colorado retreat with ski-in, ski-out access set above Beaver Creek Village. After a long day on the slopes, guests can enjoy views of the Rockies from the acclaimed Grouse Mountain Grill.

Architect Mario Botta designed the striking spa at the Tschuggen Grand Hotel in Arosa, Switzerland. The alpine retreat, which was built in 1929, features 130 rooms and suites with opulent interiors by Carlo Rampazzi.

Designed by architect Sybille de Margerie, the intimate Cheval Blanc Courchevel in Courchevel, France, is the ultimate in alpine luxury. The resort, which is owned by LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, is also filled with blue-chip artwork by Michel Othoniel, Xavier Veillant, and Bruno Peinado, whose Trojan Horse sculpture is seen here.

Founded by railway tycoon William Cornelius Van Horne in 1888, the Fairmont Banff Springs is set within Banff National Park and offers stunning views of the Canadian Rockies. The sprawling hotel, which was inspired by a Scottish baronial castle, includes 764 rooms and suites and nine restaurants and bars.

The St. Regis Aspen Resort in the Colorado Rockies received a $40 million makeover by interior architect Lauren Rottet in 2012. Set at the base of Aspen Mountain, the hotel includes 179 rooms and suites outfitted with Ralph Lauren beds and desks and marble-lined baths.

The ski-in, ski-out Hôtel des Dromonts in Avoriaz, France, was built in the 1960s by architect Jacques Labro, who was inspired by the work of Le Corbusier and Charlotte Perriand. The interiors of the distinctive angular building were recently refreshed and upgraded by designer Jocelyne Sibuet.

Munich-based firm Oikios Architect took inspiration from pine cones for the design of the AlpenGold Hotel in Davos, Switzerland. The oval façade uses over 790 curved, overlapping steel panels to create the scaled appearance. Inside, 216 tasteful guest rooms overlook the city—home to the World Economic Forum—and surrounding mountains.

Offering a unique combination of Asian-inspired design motifs and alpine rustic touches, The Chedi Andermatt is one of Switzerland’s most wonderful offerings. The boutique hotel is located 4,747 feet above sea level and includes a 25,833-square-foot spa to take advantage of when you’re not out on the slopes.

With rustic and understated architecture and interiors, Le Chalet Zanier is designed to mimic the natural beauty of the surrounding Mont Blanc mountain range. The resort is made up of a 12-room main structure as well as a separate three-bedroom private cottage. Like the snowflakes that top the roofs, no room is exactly like any of the others.

Located in a densely wooded area, Forestis is situated exactly where the Austrian monarchy established a tuberculosis sanatorium in 1912. Designed with simplicity in mind, the rich stone, wood, and glass of the hotel are inspired by the nature that surrounds it.

#4938. Unocoin keeps deposits and withdrawals halted over suspect transfers

Unocoin said the transfers were signed and broadcast outside BitGo’s platform, and BitGo said the account freeze worked as intended.

Update (Nov. 13, 2026, 12:30 pm UTC): This article has been updated to include BitGo’s response and clarify that the account freeze applied to activity routed through BitGo’s platform.

Indian cryptocurrency exchange Unocoin has kept deposits and withdrawals suspended as it investigates suspicious wallet transfers and a breach of its own systems.

BitGo froze Unocoin’s enterprise account on Nov. 6 at the exchange’s request. Unocoin said the freeze appeared to have worked as intended and that the transfers were signed and broadcast onchain outside BitGo’s platform, according to its Friday update.

“Our review found that the transaction examined was signed using the user and backup keys held by Unocoin and broadcast externally onchain, without BitGo’s participation. BitGo’s systems were not breached in connection with that transaction,” BitGo said in a statement to Cointelegraph.

The company said the freeze applied only to activity routed through its platform and that the transfers were signed using keys Unocoin held outside BitGo’s systems.

Unocoin said it was investigating possible use of the wallet’s backup signing option and whether any cryptocurrency was lost. The exchange did not respond to Cointelegraph’s request for more information before publication.

Unocoin first detected unauthorized activity on Nov. 6 and suspended all services on Monday after detecting further activity. On Thursday, it disclosed outgoing transfers from an Ethereum address associated with its BitGo wallets and said its infrastructure had been compromised.

A Nov. 5 warning from India’s cybersecurity agency described an AI-assisted campaign targeting crypto exchanges and other financial firms. No connection to Unocoin’s incident has been established.

Related: India plans first tokenized bonds using wholesale CBDC: Report

Bühler says she prioritized “unexpected, collected things that you just don’t automatically go to when you think of homeware.”

The vase is a piece Bühler keeps coming back to: “You would just be happy to have it on the table without flowers,” she says.

#4934. Israeli police arrest five in $5M WhatsApp crypto trading probe

Police suspect the group drew up fictitious loan agreements to disguise crypto trading proceeds it transferred directly into bank accounts.

Israeli police arrested five people on Tuesday in a money laundering investigation involving about 16 million shekels ($5 million) in crypto transactions arranged through a WhatsApp group.

Investigators from the National Unit for Combating Economic Crime within Lahav 433 suspect the group provided crypto services without a license and failed to report transactions to Israel’s tax authorities. Police allege the group used fictitious agreements to make crypto proceeds transferred into bank accounts look like loans, according to The Jerusalem Post.

Authorities seized wallets, computers and tens of thousands of shekels in cash while searching the suspects’ homes. Investigators questioned the five on suspicion of money laundering, fraud and providing financial asset services without a license.

Israel’s Tax Authority announced two other arrests on Oct. 6 in cases involving suspected failures to report crypto activity. One involved trades worth tens of millions of dollars. In the other, an Ashdod resident allegedly failed to report income from about $13 million in crypto trades between 2019 and 2021.

A November 2024 audit by Israel’s State Comptroller found that about 500 people reported crypto activity each year on average from 2018 to 2022, out of at least 200,000 potential filers.
