And, the color options are awesome, too—there’s more than just the black and brown if you’re like us and love a vivid pop of color in the colder months.

We also like this coat because it doesn’t make us feel like the Michelin Man (ha!), but still has ample room for layering underneath. It has a slightly snug fit, and is designed to be worn over light layers or under a bigger coat. But Nied says she could have sized down and still been comfortable, too.

What really sets this parka apart from others is the interior shoulder straps. "This little inside feature lets me easily slip my arms out of the sleeves without removing the whole jacket," she says. With other coats, she usually ends up awkwardly carrying them in a big bundle whenever she's indoors, she says. There’s also a back vent with snap closures if you get overheated but don’t want to fully take the coat off.

Some additional features: The hood is just the right size—big enough to keep Nied’s head warm without causing a hair disaster. It has multiple closures, like buttons and zippers down the front. Nied is usually a size medium, and says this coat runs true-to-size. Before buying a winter coat, think about where you’ll be using it. Are you living in a big city or a rural area? Does it get crazy cold or more temperate in the winter? How active are you? Once you've decided what you need, you can get into the nitty-gritty of coat shopping.

The key to a warm winter coat? Insulation. But there are two main types to consider: down and synthetic. Learning a bit about them can guide you in choosing the right coat for your lifestyle.

The bottom line: If you live in a wet environment and want to spend less money, go with synthetic insulation. If you live in a drier, colder place and are willing to splurge a bit more, opt for a coat that has down insulation.

You want to make sure your winter jacket is warm enough to last through many seasons. #4888. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

#4887. Joseph Dirand Joins Forces with Peter Brant and Stephanie Seymour Brant to Reimagine a Historic 1920s Palm Beach Mansion

It began with a chance encounter and a phone call. The French architect Joseph Dirand was walking into a restaurant in New York when he ran into an old friend, the art dealer Tico Mugrabi. Dirand mentioned that he was flying to Palm Beach the next day and his friend lit up. Mugrabi pulled out his phone and made a call. “Peter, my friend Joseph is coming to Palm Beach tomorrow,” Dirand recalls him saying. “You have to meet this guy.” The following day Dirand was sitting across from Peter Brant, the fabled industrialist and publisher, and his wife, Stephanie Seymour Brant, one of the defining supermodels of her generation, in their new home. The Brants had owned the house for only a few days, and it marked the opening of a new chapter for the couple.

The Brants in front of Warhol’s White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), 1963, in the great room. Jean Prouvé coffee table; sofa and chairs by Pierre Jeanneret.

Marc Newson’s aluminum Lockheed Lounge, a Tower Cabinet by Ettore Sottsass, and a Trapeze table by Jean Prouvé all stand in the loggia.

A Végétale mirror by Claude Lalanne reflects Untitled (Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman), 1980, and a 1930s settee by Jean-Michel Frank.

A pair of bespoke Philippe Anthonioz floor lamps Flank Jonathan Horowitz’s Self-portrait in “Mirror #1” (Kevin), 2012.

Brown Jordan chaise longues under umbrellas by Business & Pleasure Co. stand poolside.

There is something quintessentially American in how quickly it all unfolded, and for Dirand, it meant meeting a man he had long admired. As an inquisitive young designer he had pored over photographs of Brant’s earlier homes, and one image had stayed with him: It showed a Jean Prouvé desk beneath a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, captured at a time when almost no one thought to set French postwar design against contemporary art. “For me, Peter was a kind of collector’s hero,” says Dirand.

Brant’s eye for art and design was formed early. His father loved classical art and considered even Picasso “way too modern,” but on family ski trips to Switzerland the teenage Brant got to know the Zurich dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who subsequently introduced him to Leo Castelli, and the two titans of the art world became the young Brant’s mentors. Brant then bought his first Andy Warhol painting in 1966, and by the time Warhol’s business manager, Fred Hughes, introduced them in November 1968, he already owned about seven of them. Warhol and Brant would go on to become close friends for the remainder of the artist’s life.

In a corner of the Great Room, Roy Lichtenstein’s The Refrigerator, 1962, faces a 1960 copper hanging cabinet by Paul Evans. a 1934 plaster vase by Alberto Giacometti sits on A Joseph Dirand Edition Iseo Gold coffee table. 1950s Hirondelles wall light by Jean Royère; pair of 1958 Diego Giacometti armchairs.

Warhol’s 1975 portrait of Murray Brant (Brant’s father) commands a wall of the paneled study. Direction armchair and Présidence desk by Jean Prouvé; Ettore Sottsass hanging lamp.

Artworks in the entrance hall include, from left, a Massangis stone lion-head fountain feature by Harumi Klossowska de Rola, 2022; Andy Warhol’s Self Portrait (Green), 1964; a Klossowska de Rola wolf sculpture; and Richard Prince’s Nurses’ Dormitory, 2002. The sanded Ceppo di Gré stone modular console is by Dirand.

In the primary bedroom, George Condo’s 2004 portrait of Stephanie Seymour Brant hangs above a 1946 Charlotte Perriand sideboard on which stands an enameled earthenware lamp by Roger Capron. A Jean Prouvé Bridge armchair joins an Ours Polaire chair and sofa by Jean Royère around Prouvé’s Tripod coffee table.

An exterior view of the 1926 Addison Mizner residence

Few people then saw Warhol’s work the way Brant did. When he hung his first Marilyn at home, visitors were shocked: “People would come to my house and think, This is the worst thing I’ve ever seen. In the 1960s, he says, you could count the serious collectors of Pop art “on three hands.”

His rule, he says, is to collect “something that was in style that’s out of style,” though never as speculation. Between their holdings and those of the Brant Foundation, which he established in 1996 to promote the education and appreciation of contemporary art and design, the collection now numbers more than 3,000 works, and he has never bought for a particular wall. What he misses in many newer collections is any sense of the person behind them. “You can see right away that this guy had a great adviser,” he says, “but there’s no madness in the collection. Every collection should have some madness.”

Carlo Mollino’s Tipo B side chair rests beneath Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981.

A painting by Glenn Ligon and a stool by Shiro Kuramata in Brant’s bath

Seymour Brant and Brant in the great room

Brant has shared much of his collecting journey with Seymour Brant, whom he married in 1995. She has built a collection of her own: Her passion is clothing rather than paintings, and she has pursued it with the same scholarship and the same sharp eye as her husband. She was a close friend of the legendary couturier Azzedine Alaïa and has one of the most significant holdings of his work, alongside historic couture that Dirand describes as extraordinary. Where Brant is the storyteller, Seymour Brant is the quieter presence, though Dirand is clear that she was integral to every decision. Her collecting has even changed the way Brant sees his own. “It’s not a dress in a closet,” he says. “It’s a piece of art, and it mixes with art.”

Brant has spent some 50 years in the Palm Beach area, first as a polo player. He and Seymour Brant had no need for a new home there—they loved the one they had as their children grew up. But when Collado Hueco, a home by Addison Mizner, the architect who defined 1920s Palm Beach, came on the market in 2020, the collector in him took over. “It was a piece of history,” Dirand says. “For him, there was no choice.” Designed in 1924 for the American businessman Paul Moore, it is one of Mizner’s boldest and most unusual houses.

In a hall, a 1974 Diego Giacometti bench sits in front of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Sugar Ray Robinson), 1982. The curtain rods are by Julian Schnabel.

Warhol’s The Kiss (Bela Lugosi), 1964, and a 1947 Alexandre Noll mahogany armchair in a corner of the primary bedroom. Philippe Anthonioz hanging light; Jean Prouvé tripod coffee table; Jean Royère Ours Polaire sofa.

John Currin’s Constance Towers, 2009, presides over Seymour Brant’s dressing room. Furniture includes an Ambassador chair and Éléphanteau sofa, both by Jean Royère.

In the great room, a plaster bas-relief, Support, and a carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti are flanked by a pair of Éléphanteau chairs by Jean Royère. In the foreground is a Fondation Maeght chair by Diego Giacometti.

The house presented Dirand with a real puzzle. Asymmetrical, it spreads across multiple wings, varying from one to three levels. The main entertaining rooms had retained their original character, while the entrance and stair hall were dark and enclosed. Dirand set out to let the sunlight that moves across the house reach every part of the interior as much as possible. The collection shaped Dirand’s approach too. With so many treasured works coming into the house, the team wanted to ensure they would be protected against anything the unpredictable Florida weather could bring. What began as a renovation became, in Dirand’s words, “a reconstruction saving the historical.” Rather than demolishing and starting again, the team kept the historic walls standing, reinforced every one of them, and dug beneath to take the foundations deeper. New hurricane-proof windows were set into concrete frames, the roof was removed and rebuilt, and the original tiles and the patina of the plaster fireplace were carefully preserved. The project took about four years. Throughout, Dirand immersed himself in Mizner’s doors, ceilings, and patterns so that the new rooms would be a true homage rather than a copy.

Early on, Brant handed Dirand two thick binders, one of artworks and one of design pieces. “This is what you can use,” he said. A few days later, on holiday with his family, Dirand spread every page across the floors. “I was walking on the paper,” he says. It reversed the usual order in which the architect designs the rooms and the art arrives afterward. Here the collection came first, though never rigidly, because “a collection is also something that is alive.”

A Diego Giacometti bench and A Jean Royère Liane six-branch floor lamp in a hall

A chair and floor lamp by Diego Giacometti stand next to the fireplace in the great room.

Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981, commands a wall of the loggia. Ours Polaire chair and Yo-Yo side table, both by Royère.

A family photo and fragrance bottles line up on a windowsill in Seymour Brant’s bath.

Warhol’s Big Campbell’s Soup Can with Can Opener (Vegetable), 1962, hangs in the stairwell, which also features a Jacques Adnet wall light.

At the heart of the home are two main spaces, the great room and the loggia, which are perhaps the spaces that both Dirand and Brant are most proud of. The great room is centered around a monumental fireplace that has the grandeur of a castle. Commanding one wall is a rare carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti, nearly three meters high and crowned with a bas-relief of a female figure, made for Jean-Michel Frank’s important 1938 commission for the Born family in Argentina. It was one of a pair, and Dirand says no one knows where the other is today. Beside the fireplace hangs Warhol’s 1963 White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), one of Brant’s most recent and important acquisitions; he had wanted a Car Crash painting since the ’60s. Prouvé furniture from Brazzaville, weathered by the Congo climate, sits amid Native American and African objects, and at the center of it all is a mirror polish copper table Dirand designed himself to reflect Giacometti’s bird vase and the fireplace behind it. Brant calls the table a masterpiece.

Art in the main entrance includes, from left, pieces by Jean-Michel Basquiat, Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman, and Brice Marden. Furniture includes an Ours Polaire Chair and sofa and a kidney-shaped coffee table, all by Jean Royère, and a Charlotte Perriand stool. a 1936 Jean-Michel Frank settee stands in the background.

A glimpse into the primary bedroom, where a Jean-Michel Frank table lamp sits atop a bedside table.

A wall niche holds a 2023 ibis sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola

The loggia is lighter and more playful, and its original black, yellow, and turquoise tiled floor and Egyptian-style column capitals offer a glimpse of Mizner at his most adventurous. One of the most prominent works hanging in the room is a monumental 1981 Basquiat painting, Per Capita, which Brant bought from Annina Nosei’s memorial show for the artist. At the center of the room stands an Ettore Sottsass Tower Cabinet, designed in the early 1960s, which Dirand admits he didn’t understand at first, until Brant showed him exactly how to place it. Now he can’t imagine the room without it.

Upstairs, Dirand took down walls so that the primary bedroom runs the full width of the house, capturing light from sunrise over the ocean to sunset over the garden. In Seymour Brant’s bathroom, Estremoz marble walls are carved to evoke curtains, and beyond it lies her dressing room, an intimate boudoir. Brant’s bathroom, by contrast, is a marquetry of white and gray marble built around a pair of Glenn Ligon paintings. Dirand calls the room “minimalist ornamental.”

A 2023 flamingo sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola (one of a pair) stands on the terrace.

In Seymour Brant’s bath, François-Xavier Lalanne’s Singe II, 1999, sits between a stool by Diego Giacometti and a bespoke bench by Philippe Anthonioz.

Every piece in the house comes with a story, and Dirand heard many of them over years of breakfasts, lunches, and dinners with the couple. “Every single piece could be a book,” he says. During those conversations, the collaboration between Brant and Dirand grew into a close friendship. Brant’s other great passion is horse racing, and his formidable stable has included Sottsass, the 2020 winner of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, Europe’s most prestigious race. One day, Brant called Dirand with news: Sottsass had a son, a young thoroughbred already winning races of his own. He had named him Dirand.

#4884. Want to Turn Back the Clock? These 10 Diets May Help You Age Better

You’ve got way more options than just the Mediterranean diet.

When healthy aging is the goal, it makes sense to try everything you can to make it happen. That means doing your best to exercise regularly, keep up with doctor's appointments, and eat a well-balanced diet. You have lots of options when it comes to the last one—but it can be hard to know which of the many popular eating plans is right for you. Thankfully, new research has helped narrow the choices.

The study, which was published in Nature Communications, analyzed several different diets to see how they impacted biological aging. (Biological aging is the age of your cells, while your chronological age is how old you are.) Popular eating plans like the Mediterranean diet and the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet made the cut, of course, but several lesser-known diets did too. Here’s what to know.

Meet the experts: Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet; and Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian.

For the study, researchers analyzed data from 6,470 participants who were 30 and older. Researchers looked at some of the participants' biomarkers that correlated with biological age and compared that with information about their diets.

After analyzing the data, researchers found that healthier eating in general was linked with slower biological aging, no matter which diet people chose. Each specific eating plan offered an edge with certain perks, though. Case in point: The DASH diet (which is specifically meant to stop hypertension) had more cardiovascular benefits for biological aging, while the MIND diet (which combines the Mediterranean and DASH diets for brain health) offered cognitive perks. But researchers discovered that there were a lot of shared biological aging benefits between the different types of diets.

These are the 10 diets flagged as being good for biological aging:

All of these diets are slightly different, but there are a few common threads. "They generally emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other nutrient-dense foods," says Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet.

The diets also stress the importance of minimally processed foods, while limiting refined carbs, added sugars, and processed meats, according to Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian. "The recommended foods provide fiber, antioxidants, polyphenols, vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats that support metabolic health and help protect cells from oxidative stress and chronic inflammation," she says. Oxidative stress and chronic inflammation are both linked to a higher risk of disease, Angelone points out.

These diets also support the heart, brain, and digestive systems, says Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. "All of these things factor into the aging process and somebody's quality of life as they age," she says. "When you're eating to support these different organ systems, you support your longevity and lower your risk of disease."

There are a few things to take away from the findings, according to dietitians. One is that there isn't a single eating plan that's superior to others when it comes to longevity. "It's the overall quality of what we eat consistently that matters most, rather than following a particular diet or avoiding individual foods," Gans says.

While there are plenty of diet plans out there that claim they can help you live longer, Angelone stresses this: "Healthy aging doesn’t have to include expensive foods, supplements, or restrictive diets."

Finally, the study underscores the power of nutrition in keeping you healthy. "Our genes are not our destiny," Angelone says. "We can change the expression of our genes—genomics—with nutrition and lifestyle habits."

Supporting healthy aging with the way you eat means giving your body the fuel it requires to function well, Angelone says. "Healthy aging isn’t about finding a perfect diet or miracle food or supplement," she says. "It is about consistently providing foods that supply nutrients needed by our bodies to function optimally, repair cellular damage, and protect themselves. This will impact how we age."

#4883. Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric

Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5-8 commercial trucks. That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt. “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”

I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars (regardless of what you saw on Fox News). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time, publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

You can check out the full text of Sourcewell’s contract with Peterbilt, below, then let us know what you think of Pete’s efforts to electrify your local government fleet in the comments.

There's a big misconception that deep penetration means jackhammering or pounding away, says Ian Kerner, PhD, LMFT, a sex therapist and author of She Comes First. #4881. How to Lose Weight Naturally, According to Experts

Here are 10 easy-to-follow tips to speed up the process—and make it more enjoyable.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Starting a weight-loss journey is no easy feat. There’s a lot to think about, between getting into a regular workout routine, changing up what you eat, and maybe even considering a GLP-1 medication.

But at its core, weight loss is about developing a healthy, sustainable relationship with food and movement. You don’t have to make a dozen changes all at once—the goal is long-term success, even if it’s a slow process. That’s why you should aim to lose one to two pounds a week, says Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, a dietitian at Eat Well, Live Well. Working out at a manageable pace, eating balanced meals, and making maintainable changes can help you feel your best.

Meet the experts: Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, is a nutritionist at Eat Well, Live Well. Kami Blease, CPT, is a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. Tatyana Johnston, CPT, is a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. Jordan Hill, RD, is a nutritionist with Top Nutrition Coaching.

Ahead, experts share their 10 best tips to make your weight-loss journey successful.

First, be sure to consult your doctor—they’ll help you set mindful, attainable goals that will keep your body healthy and strong. Then, try implementing more of these habits into your lifestyle:

Take the stairs every day at work or hold a quick plank first thing in the morning. "All these things add up over time," says Kami Blease, CPT, a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. "I recommend finding things you could do almost daily.”

Additionally, try adding a brisk 30-minute walk into your day (even if it’s broken up into three 10-minute walks) to increase calorie burn and push you closer to your weight-loss goals, per the Mayo Clinic. "It's low impact and not a super strenuous form of movement, which increases the chances that someone will stick with it,” says Tatyana Johnston, CPT, a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. "Just remember to recover with hydration, fuel, and stretching.”

Burn fat and build muscle with the WH+ 4-week walking plan

Strength training “helps with balance and stability, improves metabolism, and even lowers your risk of certain diseases," says Blease. Resistance training has also been found to help with weight loss and body recomposition, according to a 2026 study in Frontiers in Endocrinology that had 304 adults follow a calorie-restricted diet and either resistance train, do aerobic exercise, or no exercise for 1 to 18 months.

To get comfortable with form, try practicing bodyweight exercises first, Blease recommends, then add weights after you’ve mastered the move. This can help you focus on progressive overload—which means gradually increasing the weight, frequency, or number of reps over time, Blease says. Eventually, you should aim to work all major muscle groups at least twice a week, per the new ACSM resistance training guidelines.

Cardio can also help with weight loss—the CDC recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (such as brisk walking) per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity (like running) each week. However, this number can vary based on someone’s individual health, and the intensity of the cardio. "Consistency is key. If you can establish and stick to a cardio schedule, you have a better chance at losing weight and keeping it off," Johnston says. Playing sports, working out with friends, or listening to a podcast during cardio can help boost your motivation too.

Also, if you enjoy high-impact exercises and want to lose weight fast, HIIT workouts can be a great way to expend a lot of energy in a short period of time. "You can ramp up the intensity by trying to get in more reps during a certain amount of time or using heavier weights while maintaining the same time goal,” says Blease. “Both will increase your intensity and continue to challenge your body."

If the gym or workout classes aren’t really your speed, choose a form of movement that you love so you can stay consistent with it. “Hiking, swimming, skiing, surfing, or biking are all forms of movement that might feel more sustainable,” says Blease.

"Start smaller than you might think," Blease says. "Often, people overcommit because they are excited. However, it's then easy to get burnt out." After a few weeks, add in a second day, and when that feels seamless, try a third, and over time, you'll find a cadence that works for you, she adds.

Just make sure you always have at least one rest day. "People can get so fixated on weight loss that they end up [overdoing exercise and] hurting themselves," Blease says. "Take time to stretch, rest, and recover as needed."

"Having a trainer create a program that is specific to your needs ensures that you are more likely to get the results you are looking for—and keep your body safe in the process," says Blease. They can help you lose fat while building muscle, which can better your overall metabolic health and insulin sensitivity, and regulate blood sugar to support a healthier body recomposition.

A trainer will also make sure you maintain proper form and that you stay consistent. Decide on a number of days per week that fits your goal and budget, and ask your trainer to help hold you accountable, Blease says.

Research suggests that working with a personal trainer may have more profound effects on weight loss: A 2024 study in Heliyon had 66 adults train individually, with a partner, or a personal trainer over 12 weeks, and they monitored their improvements in bench presses, squats, skeletal muscle mass, and fat mass. The group that worked with a personal trainer improved their leg training and reduced fat mass compared to the other groups.

Protein can help you stay full throughout the day, stabilize your blood sugar levels, and synthesize muscle mass, Smith says, helping with weight loss. While individual dietary needs vary, you can generally aim for 30 to 35 grams of protein per meal to help you stay full throughout the day. Some good sources include eggs, poultry, seafood, red meat, beans, peas, lentils, legumes, nuts, seeds, and soy, per the current Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Additionally, "fiber is more slowly digested and helps keep you feeling full for a longer period,” Smith adds, recommending vegetables. Increased vegetable intake is also linked to lower blood sugar levels, lower triglycerides, and can help promote liver function. If you don't love veggies, you can also puree them and add them to a sauce or weight-loss-friendly smoothie.

Lastly, don’t forget about healthy (unsaturated) fats—which can help provide energy, per the Mayo Clinic. Try avocados, extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, seeds, soybeans, and seafood.

"Drinking enough water can help you to feel full and prevent overeating," says dietitian Jordan Hill, RD. Aim to drink about half your body weight in ounces of hydrating fluids per day.

Also, avoid sugary beverages. "Juices, sodas, and fancy coffees are often the calorie-equivalent of a meal, yet they will still leave you hungry," says Smith. "The sugar content is often more than a candy bar, which will cause blood sugar levels to rise." Instead, replace your beverages with fruit-infused water, herbal tea, or coffee with cinnamon or zero-calorie sweeteners.

Avoid foods that are high in added sugars, unhealthy fats, and empty calories, which can contribute to weight gain, says Hill: "Instead, focus on eating whole, nutrient-dense foods that will provide your body with the nutrients it needs."

Listening to your internal cues of hunger and fullness can help you control portion sizes, which can also aid weight loss. "Honoring fullness can help prevent overeating and ensure that you're not consuming more calories than your body needs," says Hill. Keeping a food journal can also help you become more mindful of what you're eating, when, and how you're feeling throughout the process of losing weight.

“When you skip meals or go too long in between meals or snacks, you get overly hungry. This makes it much more difficult to make healthy choices, and it also makes it harder to not overeat later," says Smith. Skipping meals can also result in a slower metabolism and leave you feeling fatigued, which can negatively impact your workouts both in effort and recovery.

If you struggle to eat consistent meals, Smith recommends munching on small snacks throughout the day. “Set yourself up for success by bringing healthy snacks with you when you’re away from home, so you’re not caught in a situation where you are really hungry but have no access to healthy food,” she says.

If you need extra assistance, a dietitian can analyze your diet and recommend personalized tips for how you can eat to lose weight, which may be more helpful than doing it on your own. A 2025 review of articles on weight-loss interventions provided by a dietitian for overweight and obese adults in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics looked at how working with a dietitian improved their health markers, as opposed to not working with one (the control group). The group that worked with a dietitian had improved weight loss, waist circumference, blood pressure, and quality of life compared to the control group.

When you encounter a setback (like when you skip a few days of workouts), it can be discouraging and all-consuming, and can cause you to fall off track. "One of the most crucial components of successfully reaching a goal is to not let setbacks ruin our progress,” says Johnston. “The setback is often not as severe as we think, and will not impact our end goal very much at all.”

Just take a breath and realize we’re all human and mistakes are normal; then move forward with your health plan in mind.

And don’t forget to be kind to yourself. Practicing self-compassion and returning to your plan will help reinforce your goal and remind you that this weight-loss journey requires patience and perseverance. "Practice giving yourself grace when [you] slip up,” Johnston says. “As long as it doesn’t become a habit, you will continue moving forward towards your goal.”

#4880. How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman

Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique, it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.”

They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD.

The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery.

The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns.

The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says.

The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.”

The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum.

As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says.

Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions.

When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected  and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey.

Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.”

Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.”

In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church.

Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”)

The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork.

The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades.

The 1970s textile art in the office is a vintage find of Burns’s that Soll loves. “I used to go to Rodney’s apartment when we first started dating, and I would be like, ‘Oh my God! Like, if we break up, I’m never gonna be able to find this tapestry,’” he says.

Soll got permission from his landladies to retile the bathroom and add a new vanity. The metal Curtis Jeré artwork comes from Burns’s collection.

The bohemian architecture of the home lends quirkiness to the design. The main bedroom isn’t a perfect square, making it seem like a stainless steel bed from TTMM is placed on a diagonal but is actually following the geometry of a very funky, angular bedroom.

The couple has taken their time tinkering and adjusting the decor, taking a considered approach to collecting and combining their belongings. Soll describes the overall vibe as having an Afrocentric theme that’s also a little bit Ralph Lauren. “Our visions have mingled,” Burns says.

Still, there is one last item the couple needs to complete the design: a blanket basket. But, says Soll, “We still haven’t found one we agree upon.”

The backyard is also home to a shed (not pictured), which functions as Burns’s closet.

#4878. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Lung Cancer Can Look Like Anyone

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Picture someone with lung cancer. Now picture a 24-year-old soccer player in the prime of his life. A filmmaker in her early 40s with a camera in her hand, doing what she loves best. A busy mom of two, with a shoulder so sore she can’t pick up her newborn, yet struggling to get a diagnosis.

The gap between the picture in our heads and the people actually being diagnosed is costing time. And time is the one thing with lung cancer you cannot get back.

We know that lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the leading cause of cancer death. And while lung cancer incidence rates are falling in many countries as fewer people smoke, lung cancer in people who have never smoked is on the rise globally, both as a proportion and in absolute numbers.

According to the CDC, as many as 20% of lung cancers diagnosed in the US are in people who have never smoked. Data suggests that non-smoking lung cancer is now among the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide.

The numbers are stark. Lung cancer can affect anyone. And that includes the young – like Alex, one of the subjects of a powerful new short documentary commissioned by the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK for their Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign.

Alex was a 24-year-old soccer player who died just weeks after receiving a diagnosis of Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) positive lung cancer, following several misdiagnoses born of the fact that no one suspected lung cancer in one so young, fit, and with no smoking history. The film was made by filmmaker Sarah Li, who herself was diagnosed with Stage 4 EGFR+ lung cancer in April 2024, just a month after Alex died from the same mutation of the disease, and charts her journey with survivor’s guilt, what an earlier diagnosis may have meant for Alex, and what that fact means for her own future.

Ahead of Lung Cancer Awareness Month in November, I sat down with my friend, Gini Harrison, to talk about the film, her own journey, and why catching lung cancer sooner matters so much. Gini is a Professor of Psychology at The Open University, a trustee of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK, and is living with stage 4 EGFR-positive lung cancer. She’s also the mom at the top of this piece, whose sore shoulder was initially attributed to breastfeeding posture.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Gini Harrison: I’d had my son, Michael, in February 2021 and was on maternity leave. My daughter, Emily, was five. I think the shoulder pain started around March, but that was it. No cough, no breathlessness… nothing that made me think about my lungs.

Initially, they gave me painkillers, which helped a bit. But the pain kept getting worse. Eventually, I started losing movement and strength in my arm, and it got to the point where I couldn’t pick up my son anymore.

This was all happening during COVID, so my appointments were over the telephone. Eventually, after months without being examined face-to-face, I paid to see a shoulder specialist. As soon as he touched my shoulder blade and I practically leaped out of the chair, he knew something wasn’t right. He ordered an MRI, which showed a tumor in my shoulder blade and another in my upper right lung. In December 2021, I was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer.

Gini Harrison: I wasn’t thinking, “This must be cancer.” I was just thinking, “Why isn’t this getting better?”

And I think that distinction matters. Patients shouldn’t have to identify their own disease before they can get help. You should be able to say that something is wrong and be listened to.

Gini Harrison: It was devastating. So many of my first questions were about the children: “How are we going to tell them?” “Am I going to be here to see them grow up?” “Will they remember me?” Suddenly, there was a question mark over a future I’d taken for granted.

I was also completely shocked by the type of cancer. If someone had said breast cancer, I don’t think I would have been anywhere near as surprised. But lung cancer?! I’d always associated it with smoking, and I’d never smoked.

I hadn’t imagined that this particular cancer could ever happen to me. So yes, I had some assumptions that I now challenge. I understand how deeply rooted they are because I had them too.

Gini Harrison: People are often shocked, and one of the first questions is whether I smoked.

And they often look healthy. That doesn’t mean everything is easy, or that there aren’t side effects. It just means you can’t tell what someone is dealing with by looking at them.

I think we’ve given lung cancer such a narrow public image that people outside it can become almost invisible.

Gini Harrison: Oh, yes! Once, I spoke to a doctor about a breathing problem after radiotherapy. He asked, “How much did you smoke?” When I said I’d never smoked, he replied, “Well, how did you get lung cancer then?”

On another occasion, I went to a hospice for help managing side effects, and someone there asked, “How are you still alive?” That’s quite a thing to hear when you’ve come looking for support!

When people ask about smoking, I try to explain that I’ve never smoked and I’m certainly not alone. Never smoking doesn’t make you immune. But I’m also very clear that nobody deserves lung cancer, whether they’ve smoked or not. We shouldn’t be creating a hierarchy of who deserves compassion.

Smoking history matters medically. But in a personal conversation, “How are you doing?” is a much kinder place to start.

Gini Harrison: Lung cancer isn’t one single disease. Two people can both have lung cancer, but different changes in their cells may be driving it.

Genes contain the instructions that tell our cells how to work, including when to grow and divide. Changes in those genes (called mutations) can cause cells to keep dividing when they shouldn’t, forming a tumor. In my case, there’s a mutation in a gene called EGFR.

EGFR-positive lung cancer is a type of non-small cell lung cancer caused by a genetic mutation in the EGFR gene, which keeps the EGFR receptor switched “on,” leading to uncontrolled cell growth and enhanced cancer cell survival.

Biomarker testing looks for these changes, as well as other features of the cancer that can guide treatment. If we know what’s helping the cancer grow, there may be a medication that specifically targets it.

The word “genetic” can sound scary, particularly when you have children. But these changes usually develop in cancer cells over a person’s lifetime. They aren’t necessarily inherited.

Gini Harrison: Please get it checked. And if it persists, worsens or doesn’t improve with treatment, go back. Explain what’s changed and how it’s affecting your life. Ask, “What happens next if this doesn’t get better?”

The symptoms don’t always look like lung symptoms. Mine was shoulder pain.

Most symptoms will turn out to be something other than cancer. But when a symptom continues to worsen, the original explanation needs to be reconsidered. Lower risk doesn’t mean no risk.

And I don’t want all the responsibility to fall on patients to keep pushing. Reassurance should come with a next step.

Gini Harrison: Once I had recovered from my initial treatment, I realized that I wanted to help others in my situation, so I became a trustee of the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK. Through this work, we produced a film, Our Lungs: Time to Breathe. At the heart of it, it challenges the perception of what someone with lung cancer looks like.

The hardest part is how close to home it feels. Alex was so young, and that worked against him. Watching his family talk about what happened is heartbreaking. It’s just so unfair.

Gini Harrison: Sarah’s story shows life continuing alongside lung cancer. She’s a filmmaker with ambitions, people she loves, and things she wants to do.

Through Alex’s family, you see the enormity of the loss. I hope people feel that, rather than simply hearing another statistic.

Gini Harrison: For me, the biggest thing is that my children are growing up and I’m here to see it. Michael is now five (the age Emily was when I was diagnosed), and Emily is about to turn ten. I can’t tell you how grateful I am to be here with them.

It wasn’t about big bucket-list things. It was about being here every day. Seeing Michael start school. Seeing Emily reach double figures. Those milestones are enormous when you’ve wondered whether you’d get to see them.

After chemotherapy and radiotherapy, I’ve had no evidence of disease since May 2022, and my scans remain stable. But a big change has been seeing the progress in available treatment. It gives me more hope about what might be available if I need treatment again.

The public image of lung cancer still needs to catch up. We need better recognition of symptoms, access to appropriate testing and treatment, and support for the whole person. As a psychologist as well as a patient, I’m particularly aware that psychological well-being and family life need attention alongside the cancer itself.

Gini Harrison: I’d love for people to share the film and help get it in front of those who wouldn’t normally think lung cancer has anything to do with them. And take something from it into everyday life: book the appointment you’ve been putting off, ask your doctor about testing, or respond with kindness when someone tells you about their diagnosis.

Just being willing to rethink your assumptions could make a difference.

Gini Harrison: “You don’t have to put a brave face on with me. How are you really doing?”

When you look well, or your scans are good, people can assume you’re “fine now”. But I’m not sure the fear ever completely goes away. Every scan is terrifying. It feels like there’s a sword of Damocles hanging over my head, and part of me is waiting for the bad scan. I also still have lasting side effects from treatment, and probably always will.

My life has fundamentally changed. Some of that has brought good things, but it doesn’t make the difficult parts disappear. It helps when someone gives you room to be honest about both, without expecting you to reassure them or turn everything into a positive story.

Gini and I have been friends for nearly 30 years, and, while she’d probably cringe to hear me say it, I remain in awe of the way she approaches life with cancer. I am so grateful for her sharing her experiences with me for this column. What Gini asks of us is simple: look again, ask the question, listen, and act on your instincts. Our Lungs: Time to Breathe is where that starts for her. You can learn more about the Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign and the wider work of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK by clicking the links. — Robin Hough

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4877. The Healing Power of a Post-Divorce ‘Hoe Phase’

Many women use celibacy to process and move on from a breakup, but what if casual sex is the antidote they need instead?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Zion* was little more than a stranger when he lifted me up onto his lap in one swift movement. His hands were sure, yet soft, as he held my face, kissing me deeply. After a few moments, I pulled back, then looked down, unsure of how to respond to what I could feel was his obvious desire for sex.

I wanted him. But I was afraid I didn’t know how to do this.

Zion was the second man I’d been with since my divorce, but he was the first one I actually liked—and that I wanted to like me back.

Sensing my insecurity, Zion tipped my chin to his mouth and kissed me softer. With my legs wrapped around his waist, he picked me up and carried me to his bedroom. I threw my head back, curls wild, and giggled in a way I hadn’t in over a decade of being married.

As our bodies tangled together, our breathing synced, he looked me directly in the eyes and asked, “Are you ok? How does this feel?” I had never had a man check in with me like that.

“I feel so safe with you,” I whispered into Zion’s ear. It surprised me to know how true that was since we’d only met a few hours ago. I’d been sitting alone at a bar, as had he, and we’d struck up a casual conversation that quickly turned intimate.

I hadn’t felt safe in a long time. Not since sex with my ex-husband had become less like something I looked forward to each week and more like a duty I dreaded.

Throughout our 13-year marriage, I felt like I had expectations placed on me and my body as a wife—my husband’s “needs” often seemed to supersede my own. Consent felt implied. I didn’t think I could say “no” because that might be met with anger or coercive tactics, like begging me over and over until I relented. Each time, my sense of safety and trust eroded.

Eventually, I started recoiling from my husband’s touch because it felt like every hug or little neck rub would turn into him wanting sex.

Naturally, my libido took a nosedive. I thought the problem was me, so I went to sex therapy. But as I started to explore myself in those sessions, I realized I was still sexual. In fact, I was highly sexual. I just didn’t want to have sex with him because I always felt hypervigilant for my emotional and physical safety.

After two months of sex therapy, I asked my ex to sleep in a separate bedroom. Then, I asked for the separation that led to our divorce.

In the early stages of my separation, I was tempted to swear off sex—and men—entirely. This is not uncommon, says Laura Sgro, LCSW, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles. “Many women are like ‘screw men,’ because it’s a fear-based response,” she explains. “They’ve learned over time, especially in long-term marriages, to associate sex and intimacy with something that’s not going to be pleasurable for them, with something that’s not really their choice.”

Additionally, love and relationship coaches on social media often suggest celibacy as a way to heal after divorce and sexual trauma. But what if casual sex is the antidote many women need instead?

Once the stress of the divorce dissipated and I settled into my new life as a single mother, I just wanted to have some fun. So, I started leaving my house more often, instead of being wrapped up in “mom duties” all of the time. I went to cute cafes to work, had lunch or drinks at a bar, smiled at men who looked at me, and started conversations with people around me. That’s how I met Zion, and, well, one thing led to another…

Although I liked him—immediately—I wasn’t looking for commitment. Being someone’s partner or girlfriend didn’t sound appealing to me because I’d just escaped all the oppressive gendered expectations that had come with those labels. I just wanted to feel desired and have sex again—uninhibited, no strings attached, exploratory, and pleasurable. I wanted to be free.

Casual sex can be a way for women to take their agency back, says Alica Livingston, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in Texas. “When sex becomes their choice—who they have sex with, when they have sex, what that sex looks like—it can be an incredibly healing and powerful experience.”

It can also be an informative one. Many women don’t know what they like in the bedroom because so much of their sexual experience has been framed around their partner’s pleasure, says Sgro. Embracing casual sex after a breakup or divorce can help women center their own pleasure and regain their confidence.

But if you want to get to know your body better before jumping into bed with someone new, try some solo exploration. “Experimenting with self-touch, even non-sexually, can help women identify what they actually like and dislike,” says Sgro. She suggests touching yourself in ways you haven't tried before—light, firm, slow, still—and rate sensations as pleasant, neutral, or not for you. (For example, you might enjoy gently trailing your finger along the inside of your forearm, but want a firmer touch around your erogenous zones.) Over time, this self-exploration can expand into more sensual territory, like trying toys that offer different sensations or inviting a partner to explore further.

Sgro also recommends women find a hobby or activity that helps them connect with their bodies. “Many women feel disconnected from their bodies post-divorce, and it's so important to rebuild that connection with yourself on your terms,” she says. It can be yoga, weight lifting, dance classes—anything that helps you feel stronger, more empowered, and able to express yourself through movement.

For me, it was twerk classes. The rap music reminded me of the ’90s video vixens and my first “hoe phase” in high school. As a young woman, I had a lot of unsatisfying, performative sex out of pressure to be cool and feel chosen.

This, of course, is the argument against casual sex, and why embracing it often goes against the popular #BoySober and “decentering men” movements. These trends are not only a direct response to the violence women risk by romantically interacting with men; they are also evidence of the humiliating and lackluster dating dynamics we face now—breadcrumbing, micro-cheating, future faking, monkey branching (the Gen Z-informed list goes on).

It’s also true that more women than men experience postcoital dysphoria and regret after one-night stands, booty calls, and casual sexual encounters. But this isn’t just another case of the classic gender gap—it’s due to a variety of factors, not least of which is sexual satisfaction.

But casual sex that is intentional, focused on self-exploration, and re-centers your pleasure can take off the pressure to perform or please your partner, says Sgro.

Now that I was in my late 30s, I was determined that my second “hoe phase” would be all about me and what I wanted. For starters, I wrote down my “Hell Yes” and “Hell No” lists. It was an easy and straightforward way for me to figure out what I liked in bed, what I wanted to try, and what I wasn’t open to. I also used sexting to get more comfortable sharing my desires and boundaries with new partners, which was great practice for having those conversations in person.

For me, having a post-divorce “hoe phase” was exactly what I needed. I started having the best sex of my life, including with Zion. He was the first man I saw myself with post-divorce, but neither of us were ready for a commitment at the time, so our connection only lasted a few weeks. For the next three years, I entertained many casual romantic and sexual connections. Eventually, I realized that while having no-strings-attached sex was great, I love monogamy and would like to get married again. So, earlier this year, I started seriously dating someone else.

Unfortunately, it didn’t work out, and I recently became single again. Part of me wonders if I should have another “hoe phase”? Or, should I stay away from random men until I find my husband?

Sgro says any woman going through a divorce or a breakup should ask herself these kinds of questions—and be honest in her answers. “If you want casual sex, give yourself that permission to explore it in a way that feels good for you,” she says. “And if you’re not ready for that, that’s OK too. No one makes the rules except you.”

So, I don’t know if I’ll continue to embrace casual sex, take some time to explore celibacy, or perhaps return to a past romance. What I do know is that my “hoe phase” opened possibilities—for more autonomy and more pleasure. And maybe even love.

Sarah Gallucci is the author of Laid: A Memoir of Love, Sex, and Marriage. She has written reported features for CNN, The Atlantic, The Washington Post, Harper's Bazaar, among others. She has given two TEDx talks and hosts writing workshops around the world. To read more check out her website: www.SarahGallucci.com.

#4875. 17 Best Airbnb Cabins for a Picture-Perfect Outdoor Retreat (2026)

Picture this: A wood-burning stove, a claw-foot tub, no cell service, and no news. Are you in heaven? Or are you in one of the best Airbnb cabins we’ve rounded up across the US? Whether it’s an organic design marvel in Washington that would make Frank Lloyd Wright weep or a sauna-equipped “bird house” cabin in Wisconsin that piques your interest, there are so many places to enjoy the great outdoors in style. So, if immaculate cabin rentals make up your fall and winter travel mood board, look to these cozy cabins, tiny homes, chalets, and comfortable cottages for a weekend getaway. Think: elevated A-frames and Lincoln log-style beauties, fleshed out with curated amenities and thoughtful design details. Here, you can get a little lost in the beauty of the wilderness (without giving up too much in the way of modern accommodations).

Perks: Indoor fireplace, private patio, barbecue grill, sound system, security system, free parking

A steeply pitched roof and black metal siding give this tiny cabin near Oregon’s Mount Hood a striking silhouette against the towering pines. Designed by a professional architect, the 190-square-foot retreat takes its cues from shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice of forest bathing. The exterior pairs dark metal with warm pine cladding, while oversized windows look out to picturesque woodland views. Inside, there's a sound system, queen bed, wood-burning stove, and compact kitchenette, but the real luxury is falling asleep to natural white noise from the surrounding forest. Even the shower comes with a forest view, making this a particularly appealing place to spend a weekend off the grid. From $381 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, forest views, private balcony, fireplace, fire pit, nearby hiking trails, nearby skiing, private security

At nearly 11,000 feet above sea level, this Breckenridge cabin puts you practically eye to eye with Colorado’s towering Quandary Peak. Getting there involves climbing about 60 steps through the evergreens, but the payoff is a private balcony with sweeping mountain views. Inside, the renovated retreat has a Scandinavian-inspired aesthetic, with warm wood finishes, cozy textiles, and a gas fireplace for snowy evenings. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, while outside, a firepit offers another spot to take in the alpine scenery. Downtown Breckenridge is just 15 minutes away, though between the mountain views and the deck, there’s plenty of incentive to stay put. From $365 per night.

Perks: Mountain view, wood-fired hot tub, indoor fireplace, fire pit, private backyard, hiking, free parking

The Blue Ridge Mountains are the main attraction at Doah House, a cabin perched high above Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. A 16-foot wall of sliding glass doors opens onto a wraparound deck, making the one-of-a-kind forest views visible from anywhere in the living room. Inside the blonde wood interiors, a wood-burning stove, heated floors, and a lofted bedroom equipped with a queen-sized bed add to the appeal. The bathroom features Moroccan tile, a rainfall shower, and a floor-to-ceiling window overlooking the trees. Outside, a private wood-fired hot tub and firepit make a strong case for spending the evening at the cabin, though Shenandoah National Park, Appalachian Trail hikes, and local wineries are all within reach. From $204 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, hot tub, sauna, fire pit, wood-burning stove, BBQ grill, heated bathroom floors free parking

Fresh eggs from the chicken coop, herbs picked straight from the garden, and a creekside sauna are just a few of the unexpected perks at Firelight at Shope Creek, a collection of eight cabins spread across 22 wooded acres outside Asheville, North Carolina. Cozy flourishes fill this 650-square-foot retreat with modern design, like a wood-burning stove, heated bathroom floors, and a spacious deck overlooking the surrounding mountains and meadows. There's also a private hot tub just steps from the king-size bedroom, ideally positioned for stargazing after dark. Guests can wander the property's private hiking trails, gather around the communal firepits, or settle into the covered outdoor pavilion, which has its own fireplace. And despite the secluded setting, downtown Asheville and the Blue Ridge Parkway are only about 20 minutes away. From $320 per night.

Perks: Hiking trails, swimming, hot tub, fire pit, sound system, fireplace, washer/dryer

During the day, a generous amount of sunlight pours into this secluded Maine cabin, illuminating thoughtful architectural details like floor-to-celing wood paneled walls and heightened ceilings. After sunset, a well-curated lighting scheme sets the mood, affording the opportunity to test-drive the property’s record player sound system and transform the main living area into a vinyl listening den. Don’t expect to spend all your time indoors, though. Outside of this modern cabin, there’s no shortage of adventures to explore, from swimming in the lake to hiking one of several nature trails close by. Boating rentals and the local golf course offer even more ways to spend your stay, as well as winter skiing or snowboarding just a 40-minute drive away. From $645 per night.

Perks: Ocean view, shared outdoor pool, sauna, fireplace, beach access

Private and serene, sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean surround this Sea Ranch cabin escape that meets the California coast. Best suited for a couples getaway or a duo vacation, an open floor plan and 30-foot-high ceilings ensure that the space doesn’t feel overly cramped, while oversized windows drench the rental in sunlight on cloudless days. Modern upgrades like minimalist furniture silhouettes, recognizable decor, and an updated kitchen bring contemporary flair to the home’s original timber frame built back in 1965. Outside, an expansive deck overlooking the nearby meadow is a natural place to enjoy morning coffee or your current novel. Walk along the bluff to one of several bordering beaches, or visit one of the private recreation centers to work on your tennis backhand or swimming skills indoors. From $681 per night.

Perks: Lake view, fireplace, BBQ grill, fire pit, free parking, washer/dryer

Tucked among the Wisconsin woodlands, MetalLark Tower is surrounded by impressive views, supplied by the nearby wildflower meadow and clandestine lake. The 800-square-foot home’s interiors are equally noteworthy, following modern Scandinavian design principles that make the space feel intentional and cozy. (Think: simple furniture silhouettes and a neutral color palette with light wood tones contrasted by stark black and grey accents). When you’re not admiring the dramatic floor-to-ceiling windows with stunning, 360-degree views of the region, the outdoor living area has lots to offer, like a lounge area, fire pit, and grill. From $379 per night.

Perks: Outdoor showers, hot tub, fire pit

Checking into this tree-flanked cabin in Wartburg feels like stepping into a luxurious nature retreat. Maybe it’s the pair of waffle robes hung outside the private hot tub deck, or the modern Adirondacks arranged around the fire pit facing the tree line. But that’s just the beginning of the relaxation you’ll experience in your secluded private rental. Here, sliding doors and windows invite you to commune with the great outdoors from every room, while the clean, Scandinavian-style interiors align with the space’s overwhelmingly calming atmosphere. Consider staying here for a honeymoon, a romantic winter getaway, or a restful solo trip down south. From $219 per night.

Perks: wood barrel stove, sauna, access to 20 acres of land

Nothing says cabin quite like fire pits, fireplaces, saunas, and firewood: all key features of this off-grid cabin. Located in a rural, wooded area in New Hampshire, the 196-square-foot space is modest but well-stocked for seasoned outdoor travels. It runs on solar power, and features a kitchenette with a burner and butane stove as well as a private bathroom with a compostable toilet. It feels more like a campsite than a standard rental as you won’t have hot water or a refrigerator, but the simpler life does come with at least one special perk: You can sweat your stress away inside the wood barrel sauna. From $283 per night.

Perks: Sauna, fire pit, hot tub, washing machine and dryer

The fittingly named Bird House is a vision of Scandinavian restraint in Cascade, Wisconsin. It’s close to the cross-country ski trails of the nearby Kettle Moraine region, in case you need a quiet place to settle in after a day of adventure, and approximately one minute down the road from a winery known for its French-inspired vineyards. Glou glou! The property itself packs in a small kitchen and living area with a wood-burning stove, plus a serene bedroom and laundry room upstairs. A path trailing away from the house also leads you to a compact, infrared sauna that fits up to four people. For even more coziness, consider lighting up the fire pit outdoors or stepping into the bubbling hot tub on the back deck. From $305 per night.

Perks: Walk-in shower, outdoor deck, BBQ, fire pit,

Hi-vis SMEG appliances and colorful fiberglass chairs punctuate the white-walled, barebones look of this Scandi-inflected home in upstate New York. The small one-bedroom is linked to the property next door by a shared backyard and deck, so it’s a good opportunity to coordinate with a pal or two if you’re able to secure both places at once. In the mornings, sunlight streams in through the skylight overhead to bathe the place in warmth, while at sundown, the surrounding forests in Hunter invite you to tee up the outdoor fire pit and take it all in. From $218 per night.

Perks: full-service kitchen, hot tub, BBQ grill

The term “cozy” is often synonymous with “small.” Not so in this jaw-dropping A-frame that sleeps 10 of your luckiest pals. Surrounded by miles of woods, the location sets the stage for a tranquil escape, but those who are looking for a few activities to pass the time will be happy to discover its proximity to the Rockbridge Nature Preserve, as well as local wineries and breweries. While the white shiplap interior, floor-to-ceiling windows, and floating staircase create an airy feel, there’s also plenty of texture among the leather, wood and rattan furnishings to warm things up. From $882 per night.

Perks: rainfall shower, wood-burning fireplace

Visitors to this New England town—known to be one of the best ski areas on the East coast—often come to hit the slopes. But even those who have no interest in venturing outside on a cold winter day will relish their visit if they stay at this Scandinavian-inspired cabin. Light wood beams and moldings, thick rugs underfoot, and minimalist furnishings tempt even the most dedicated skiers to stay indoors. While you’re holed up in your new lodgings, enjoy a blissful soak under the rainfall showerhead or take in the view from the glass wall in the bedroom that offers an unobscured view during leaf-peeping season and beyond. From $545 per night.

Perks: outdoor patio, fully-stocked kitchen, luxury linens

An hour outside Boise, situated among the Rocky Mountains, lies a magical escape where you can leave all your stress on the car ride up. This A-frame cabin features luxury amenities, stylish furniture, and views for days (you can choose whether to enjoy them through the floor-to-ceiling windows or while relaxing in the hot tub on the deck). The wide-open, marble countertop kitchen is ideal for dining in with a hearty meal, while the circle of outdoor Adirondacks are the ideal place to gather after dark around the fire pit. From $225 per night.

Perks: dog-friendly, hot tub, indoor hammock

Perched above a river on a granite ledge, the amazing views are the cherry on top when it comes to this two-bedroom hideaway. Don’t sleep on the curb appeal—the asymmetric A-frame structure of the home is only the beginning of your visual journey. Inside, warm wooden walls, one-of-a-kind furniture, an indoor hammock, and a marble-clad shower await. The home is a 30-minute drive from the Mountain Loop Highway, which grants access to outdoor adventures in Big Four Ice Caves, Lake Twenty-Two, Heather Lake, and Gothic Basin, to name a few. From $466 per night.

Perks: Sound system, indoor fireplace, waterfront views

For a weekend getaway from NYC that isn’t the Catskills or Adirondacks, try the Easy A—a gorgeously appointed A-frame cabin just about a three-hour drive away on the Delaware River. This creekside property, located in the Pocono Mountains in Pennsylvania, was recently renovated with inspired decor choices like the oxblood and sky blue kitchen tiles. The entire cabin sleeps six and features indoor fireplaces and an outdoor fire pit for extra cozy stargazing at night. From $725 per night.

Perks: Electric vehicle charging, pontoon style rental, modern open kitchen

The entire interior of this two-bedroom cabin in northwestern Wisconsin deserves a round of applause, but it’s the full-size kitchen and its massive portal to the surrounding forest that we can’t stop thinking about. With some cabins, you’re sacrificing space for a larger living area (preferably centered around a fireplace)—the kitchen is often an area that gets overlooked in footprint. But not here; fully stocked with Instagram-worthy dinnerware, the dinner table easily becomes a place for refueling… and playing games… and catching up over morning coffee. The list goes on. When the weather agrees, head down to the lake for a dip. From $287 per night.
