#4874. Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think

For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.

The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.

The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.

Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.

And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.

Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.

The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018, the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.

That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line. And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.

Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.

Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.

They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?

So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.

Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.

It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.

It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.

Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.

Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.

And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.

Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.

Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.

But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.

Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.

And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.

Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.

Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.

And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.

Living in SE Asia this all sounds very strange. The vast majority of the worlds bikes are not owned as toys, they are the main form of transport for the family. I agree with a lot of the article but Asia is already years ahead. The fuel shortages and sky high prices are pushing people electric far faster than riders are "aging out"

But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.

That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.

Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.

In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.

#4873. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4872. 35 Best Home Gym Equipment Items to Build Your Gym, Tested By Us

This gear will make you never want to leave your personal fitness sanctuary.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHETHER YOU'RE A weightlifter, CrossFit acolyte, cardio junkie, or yoga lover, a dependable home gym setup is a must. You might not have the square footage or budget to create a space that replicates your go-to health club or weight room space, but you can still achieve great workouts at home with the best home gym equipment.

Building your home fitness setup should prioritize space, functionality, and usability over trends. Choose gear that suits your needs and storage space. Whether it's a full-on garage gym or portable equipment, the best home gym equipment can help you make the most of your home workouts.

Read more: How Men's Health Thoroughly Tests and Reviews Fitness Products

From traditional heavy lifting (we love these barbell sets and weight benches) to HIIT workouts (this 15-minute interval workout is sure to make you sweat) to full-on indoor cardio rigs (like the best indoor rowing machines and the best ellipticals), we've tested and vetted something out there for every type of training imaginable. In fact, we've used hundreds of pieces of equipment throughout the years, from the most high-end, commercial-grade options all the way down to budget gear from Amazon. Our extensive testing process has involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors, including durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value, to ensure that we recommend only the best.

SMRTFT’s Nüobell is the perfect ultra-durable adjustable dumbbell for my home workouts. It can easily be five pounds, perfect for warm-up work, or 80 pounds, enough to challenge most people on fundamental leg moves, Eric Sung, C.S.C.S., a member of the Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative and trainer at Performance Lab in New York City, told us.

These adjustable dumbbells give you the convenience of 16 sets of dumbbells all in one compact footprint. They're easy to use and offer superior durability thanks to their machined steel weight plates. If you're starting a home gym from scratch or live in tight confines with little room to spare, consider these a must-have. Few items pack as much versatility and return on investment in such a small package.

PowerBlock is practically synonymous with adjustable dumbbells—and for good reason. The Pro 100 model is compact, rugged, and replaces an entire weight rack. With a range from 5 to 100 pounds, it offers more versatility than almost any other dumbbell on the market.

One of our testers, Maillard Howell, who tried PowerBlock’s Pro 50 model, said he liked how compact the dumbbells were and that the square shape lets you set them down without rolling away. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., likes how easy they are to adjust. He’s also dropped these dumbbells from about four feet and reported zero breakage (though we wouldn’t suggest dropping them).

There’s not much to nitpick with these dumbbells. That said, they can feel awkward and obtrusive during specific exercises. For example, because your hand and wrist are inside the bell, they can feel clunky during dumbbell curls. Samuel says the weight distribution differs between PowerBlocks and traditional dumbbells, and he sticks with the latter for most accessory movements (biceps curls, skull crushers, lateral raises, etc.).

We dubbed this bench the “mid-range bench that delivers big value”. For around $350, we’re confident the AB-3000 is nicer than any bench you’ve used in a commercial gym and can serve most lifters for years. It offers flat, incline, and decline options, which most adjustable benches on the market don’t. You’ll never outlift the 1,000-pound weight capacity, and the redesigned 2.0 version features a longer back leg to eliminate side-to-side wobble.

“Hands down, my favorite feature is the ladder-style adjustment system—you can drag the bench to any upright angle in seconds,” says NASM-certified personal trainer and product tester Andrew Gutman.

There are a few trade-offs. The 2.1-inch pad gap, while common among adjustable benches, could bother some lifters if their hips land in the gap mid-set. The bench also can’t be stored upright, and at nearly five feet long, it claims a chunk of floor space. Lastly, while $350 is a fair price for this level of quality, it’s not exactly pocket change.

Read More: Our Review of the Rep Fitness AB-3000

Hammer Strength (by Life Fitness) outfits weight rooms for elite organizations—from the Tennessee Titans to Team USA Bobsled. And for good reason: When it comes to quality, dependability, and customization, Hammer Strength sets the gold standard. Even the Men’s Health weight room features Hammer Strength’s Elite iD Half Rack.

The HD NX rack is highly customizable. You can choose between two heights (86" or 91"), two storage depths (15" or 21"), and either four or six uprights. It's essentially a commercial-grade system adapted for home use. That is if your “home gym” resembles a college weight room. Before buying, measure your space carefully and consider your long-term training plans. Even in its slimmest configuration, the HD NX commands serious square footage.

But with that footprint comes unmatched functionality. You can outfit it with almost anything: multiple pull-up bar variations, band pegs, barbell storage, Nordic curl attachments, and more. The rack works with a wide range of accessories and is built to withstand hard workouts year after year.

The HD NX is the best rack money can buy, but you’ll need a lot of it. It’s overkill for most lifters, but for those building the ultimate home gym with no budget restrictions, this is the crown jewel. It’s a lifetime investment you’ll never regret.

Foldable squat racks are a game-changer for home gyms, and Titan’s T-3 Series rack offers one of the best values. When not in use, it folds flat to just five inches off the wall. Unfolded, it gives you the option of 21” or 41” of depth, with a substantial 1,100-pound weight capacity, more than enough for even serious lifters. It also comes with J-hooks (essential for racking your barbell) and a pull-up bar for added versatility.

This space-saver does come with trade-offs. Like most folding racks, it requires wall mounting, and the necessary hardware isn’t included. You’ll also want to make sure your wall can support both the 145-pound rack and the load you plan to lift. Even when mounted properly, a wall-mounted rack may feel less stable than a fully bolted-down or freestanding unit.

That said, for under $400 shipped (and with a one-year warranty), the T-3 delivers beyond its price point. It’s a no-frills, budget-friendly rack that doesn’t skimp on strength or functionality, ideal for anyone building a legit home gym in limited space.

This seven-foot Olympic barbell has been one of our favorite home barbells for years. The 15" sleeves are designed with snap clips to accommodate any 2-inch Olympic plates. It's built of 110,000 PSI tensile strength cold-rolled Japanese steel with a black oxide finish, so it's plenty durable. It's durable enough, in fact, to be rated to 1,000 pounds. That won't quite accommodate powerlifters, but it's more than enough for beginner to intermediate home lifters.

Most reviewers say it feels great in the hands (even without the knurled grip), though some report more bending than expected when lifting 350 pounds or more. But at roughly half the price of most premium alternatives, it's an incredible value, especially for any moderate weightlifters looking to upgrade their home gym without spending a small fortune.

REP Fitness' rubber bumper plates strike a strong balance of affordability and durability. Built with stainless steel inserts for easy loading and a stylish black high-density rubber, these plates are designed to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

For those looking for a complete set, with color coding for different weights, REP Fitness also offers one with five different plates—10 lb (grey), 15 lb (black), 25 lb (green), 35 lb (yellow), and 45 lb (blue)—and for the cost of $775, you can get everything you need to get started. We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these REP Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

CAP Barbell's cast iron plates strike the right balance between affordability and durability. Built with a precision-machined 2-inch center hole for a secure fit on Olympic barbells. The plates feature a durable black baked enamel finish and are built to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

For those looking for a complete set, with color coding for different weights, Titan also offers four additional plates—10 lb (grey), 25 lb (green), 35 lb (yellow), and 45 lb (blue)—and for the cost of $518, you can get everything you need to get started. We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these Titan Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

Adjustable dumbbells save space, but nothing beats the feel of individual iron in your hands. Fixed dumbbells are sturdier, more durable, and have fully knurled chrome handles for a secure, grippy feel—especially when sweating through a tough set. They’re also better suited for circuit-style training, since you don’t need to adjust weights between exercises.

REP Fitness’s Hex Dumbbell Set delivers commercial-gym quality for your home. You can choose from three weight ranges (5-50 lbs, 5-75 lbs, or 5-100 lbs) and pair them with a sleek rack in black, red, or blue. We especially love the chrome handles: They’re knurled end to end for a grippy, no-slip feel that feels premium.

That said, a complete dumbbell set takes up space. Lots of space. The 100-pound set weighs more than 2,000 pounds and spans about six feet of horizontal real estate. It's also not cheap. But if you want the real gym experience at home, these dumbbells are built to outlast your training career.

This adjustable kettlebell from Titan Fitness is “best for beginners” because it nails the fundamentals: It’s reasonably priced (around $150), adjusts from 10 to 40 pounds in seconds, and takes up the same amount of space as a pair of shoes. The weight range covers most beginner-friendly kettlebell movements—from presses and rows to goblet squats, curls, and even cleans and snatches.

If you’re a casual lifter looking to mix in the occasional kettlebell finisher, this one will serve you well. That said, more experienced users will quickly bump against the 40-pound ceiling, especially for swings and deadlifts. And while the plastic housing is sturdy, it doesn’t match the longevity or feel of solid cast iron.

Still, for anyone just getting into kettlebell training, this is the best entry-level option on the market—and a smart way to add variety without cluttering your gym.

Read More: The 6 Best Adjustable Kettlebells

Austin-based Kettlebell Kings has become a small powerhouse in the world of home gym equipment—and these powder-coated models are no exception. Made from single-cast iron with a smooth-yet-grippy powder coat finish, these kettlebells are built to withstand endless swings, snatches, and cleans. The 18 available weight options (ranging from 9 to 106 pounds) make it easy to scale up over time, and the color-coded bands around the handles let you identify weights at a glance.

That quality comes at a cost. Kettlebell Kings’ kettlebells sit at the higher end of the price range—expect to pay around $500 for a full set. But if you want top-tier, American-made bells that’ll last forever, start here. "Whether I’m repping through a set of swings or snatches, I know I can depend on the durable, powder-coated weights," says MH Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM.

Metal kettlebells are pricey. And they’re not exactly gentle on your wrists or floors. GoRuck’s Sand Kettlebell is a soft-sided alternative built for tough workouts and easy transport. Shaped like a traditional kettlebell, this canvas training tool can be filled with sand (not included), emptied when not in use, and folded up for on-the-go sessions.

It’s rugged as hell. The double-seal filling system keeps sand from leaking mid-workout. The padded handles add comfort, and GoRuck uses double-pass stitching and a reinforced base to keep the bag from falling apart, even after years of swings, presses, throws, and drops.

Just know this isn’t a direct substitute for a cast-iron bell. If you’re training for kettlebell sport or focusing on technique-heavy movements like snatches or Turkish get-ups, this won’t replicate the same feel. But for general strength and conditioning, it’s a versatile, joint-friendly, and durable option at a fraction of the price.

Plyo box workouts are a great way to build explosive strength, but not at the expense of your shins. REP’s soft plyo boxes feature a wood core and a high-density foam exterior wrapped in grippy vinyl, offering a good balance of structure and comfort.

They come in three heights—16, 20, and 24 inches—and arrive fully assembled. The soft covering helps muffle noise and reduces injury risk if you miss a rep. And while they’re relatively lightweight, each box can handle up to 400 pounds, making them suitable for bigger athletes or weighted jump work.

One thing to note: These boxes aren’t ideal on slick surfaces like tile, polished wood, or smooth concrete. They need some grip to stay put during explosive movements (we’ve made this mistake before). Also, the narrow footprint may feel less stable during lateral movements or box step-overs.

Still, for most home gym users, the REP Plyo Boxes offer a safer, quieter, and more versatile upgrade over the typical wooden box.

Read More: The 7 Best Plyo Boxes According to Certified Trainers

The Hydrow Wave earned a spot on our 2025 Men's Health Home Gym Awards. It pairs a sleek, compact design with surprisingly tranquil, waterway-inspired workouts. Unlike traditional rowers that use noisy air resistance (looking at you, Concept2), the Hydrow Wave uses magnetic resistance for a whisper-quiet ride that won’t disturb the rest of the house.

Yes, it’s pricey. And yes, you’ll need a monthly subscription. But Hydrow’s instructor-led, on-the-water sessions are so vivid and immersive that even longer workouts fly by. Samuel said it feels like you’re actually on the water, and his workouts rarely felt boring on this rower. When your workout is over, just fold it up and store it vertically to save space.

Our only gripe? You can’t skip the scenic classes and program your own intervals. Still, for most users, the guided experience is the main appeal. And when you’re done, the Wave folds upright for easy storage.

The Concept2 RowErg is the standard by which all rowing machines are measured, a device that can redline your heart rate in minutes and is perfect for strengthening hips, glutes, back, and core.

The RowErg with Standard Legs is the new name for Concept2's RowErg rower, and it's the first device that comes to mind when we think of training on a rower at home. Our editors have never been on a better rower than this one, point blank. In a nutshell, it offers many of the same features as the best rowing machines that cost twice as much.

"It's an industry standard used by CrossFit and in many high-profile competitions for a reason," Samuel says. "It relies on a variable resistance flywheel that provides a constant challenge, making it great for high volume or experienced rowers."

It's also extremely easy to assemble (you can see a video of us assembling it here). In our experience (and many Amazon reviewers agree), setup takes around 20 minutes with minimal tools or hardware (just eight screws are required). City dwellers and space-conscious users will appreciate the clever design that lets this machine separate into two pieces for easy storage. Built-in caster wheels make setup and put-away a breeze. Plus, it's surprisingly affordable. This is the definitive home rowing experience.

You can spend $25, $70, even $150 on a jump rope. But you don’t have to. After testing dozens, Men’s Health editors agree: The $6 BOOMIBOO Skipping Rope offers the best bang for your buck. It’s lightweight, durable, and surprisingly smooth thanks to ball-bearing rotation in the handles.

I’ve used this rope regularly for over a year, and it’s held up better than expected. The bearings spin clean, and the foam handles are easy on the hands. My only issue with it is that the length feels a bit off out of the package. You can adjust it (it comes at 9 feet), but I never bothered. I just widened my arms, and it still did the job.

Unless you’re chasing double-unders or elite-level speed, this rope is more than enough—and the price is tough to beat.

Read More: Best Jumping Ropes, Tested By Us

This adjustable weighted jump rope is made of thick silicone that is soft, sweat-resistant, and comfortable for long workouts. Our testing confirms this jump rope is built to last. Out of the box, it's nearly 10 feet long, but is designed to be cut to achieve the perfect fit based on user height. This is ideal for a single user, but doesn't lend itself well to multiple users within the same household unless they're the same height.

Together, the rope and handles weigh 1 pound, so this kit is enough to challenge you during a good cardio sesh. At around $20, this is another great budget-friendly option for anyone looking to get in some cardio at home without a huge piece of equipment.

When you're looking for an exercise bike that's as high-tech as it gets, the Peloton Bike is still our go-to choice. The 22-inch HD touchscreen display is crisp and easy to use, and its library of best-in-class instructor-led studio-style classes is a true game-changer for home workouts. Our editors have used this bike for more than four years now, and have never run out of fresh classes to try.

For nearly $1500, it's a bummer that users need to shell out an additional $24/month for full access to the platform. But for the many Peloton users who have found community in their classes and on the leaderboard, the cost is more than worth it.

Read More: The Best Exercise Bikes, Tested by Us

Manual treadmills may look intimidating, but they have surged in popularity for good reason: They make you work harder, respond instantly to your pace, and run quieter than motorized options. The REP Fitness Strive Treadmill is a standout in the category; it’s a durable curved treadmill that honors its promise as a manuel treadmill and adds a sled push to the equation.

At over 418 pounds, we suggest building this treadmill where you want it and avoid moving it up and down stairs. Still, built-in front wheels let you reposition it if needed. The 400-pound weight capacity makes it a solid pick for larger users, and REP Fitness backs its promise with a 5-year frame warranty—essentially guaranteeing long-term durability.

Yes, it’s big. Yes, it costs almost $4,000. But for runners or serious home gym owners looking for a low-maintenance, high-performance machine, the Strive Treadmill is a wise investment.

NordicTrack is a giant in the treadmill game, and the T10 hits the sweet spot for home gym owners. It’s more compact than the brand’s Commercial 1750, yet still boasts a full-size 60-inch running belt—long enough for sprinting and tall runners alike. Plus, it folds up for easier storage between workouts.

Despite its smaller footprint, the T10 packs in features. You can run up to 12 mph (a 5:00-mile pace) and incline up to 12%. The 10-inch touchscreen pairs with iFit for trainer-led classes, and the Follow Trainer mode automatically adjusts your incline and speed in real time to match the instructor’s terrain.

SmartAdjust learns your fitness level and tailors your workouts based on how you train, while ActivePulse adjusts intensity based on your heart rate (if paired with a compatible monitor). It’s a smart, sturdy, and space-conscious treadmill that’s ideal for intermediate to advanced runners who want a guided experience at home.

Are you aiming to build muscle like a Greek god or shed those pesky love handles? Different goals call for different equipment. If you're into strength training, focus on getting some quality adjustable dumbbells or a full rack setup. For cardio enthusiasts, a treadmill, stationary bike, or rowing machine will get your heart pumping and your sweat dripping.

Unless you're living in a mansion, your home gym likely won't be as spacious as a commercial one. So choose equipment that fits your available space. If you're tight on space, consider compact options like resistance bands or adjustable dumbbells. They're small but mighty, perfect for those who need to optimize their space.

And quality matters, man! Don't skimp on the good stuff. You want equipment that can handle your beastly workouts without falling apart like a house of cards. Look for trusted brands that have a reputation for durability and longevity. Read reviews, ask around, and do your homework. You don't want wobbly machines or weights that crack under pressure. Go for sturdy materials and solid construction. You'll be glad in the long run.

It may be the spice of life, but contrary to what the market may tell you, the basics let you perform the largest variety of movements. Pass on over-specialized tools that let you do a few unique exercises and nothing more. Dumbbells and kettlebells let you do a mix of explosive and controlled isolation moves and can help you build strength, power, and mobility. Opt for those over stability balls and suspension trainers, which require fancier setups (especially if you're building a living room facility).

Set a budget and stick to it. Home gym equipment comes in a wide range of price points, and it's easy to get carried away. Determine how much you're willing to spend and prioritize your purchases accordingly. Remember, it's better to invest in a few quality pieces than to clutter your space with cheap, flimsy gear that won't stand the test of time.

As the Fitness and Commerce Editor at Men's Health, I test and evaluate the best home gym equipment. I collaborated with our team of fitness editors and certified trainers to identify the best home gym equipment worthy of a recommendation, both new and tried-and-true. We spent months hands-on vetting products from top fitness brands, including cardio machines, weights, connected fitness gear, and more.

In fact, we've tested hundreds of pieces of equipment over the years, from the highest-end, commercial-grade models to budget gear from Amazon. Our extensive testing process involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors, including durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value, to ensure that we recommend only the best. To gather diverse perspectives, we consulted our MH Advisory Board and Strength in Diversity trainers, who shared valuable feedback on the top home gym equipment based on their expertise and experience.

Here are 35 can't-miss items we would include in our dream home gym, with picks that work for just about every space and training style.

So, you're thinking about setting up your very own home gym. Well, buckle up because it's going to be a game-changer.

Convenience is the name of the game. No more wasting precious time commuting to the gym or waiting for your turn on the bench. With a home gym, you're the boss of your own fitness kingdom. You can squeeze in a workout whenever it suits you, whether it's before the crack of dawn or after a long day at work, or in bite-sized bits between meetings. Plus, no more crowds or sweaty gym rats hogging the equipment. It's just you, your favorite tunes, and some iron to conquer.

Sure, creating a lasting home gym demands an initial investment, but it's a wise long-term savings strategy.

Consider adjustable dumbbells (priced between $400 and $800), a yoga mat (typically $20 to $140), and a cardio machine like a rower or bike (average cost around $2000). While that initial investment may seem steep, keep in mind that the average gym membership in the U.S. is about $55/month, plus initiation and cancellation fees. You'll recoup your investment in less than 5 years.

There's nothing worse than investing in a new piece of home gym equipment, only to find it's a one-trick pony you're bored with after a week. For an at-home setup that will keep you excited to use it, you want gear versatile enough to work in different ways. That way, you can keep your space uncluttered and your budget on-point.

When it comes to the best bang-for-your-buck, value-packed equipment, our answer might annoy you. But all you really need? A pair of reliable adjustable dumbbells, a training program, and a weight bench.

Top it off with a non-slip yoga mat like Lululemon's The Reversible (Un) Mat for a sweat-proof surface for floor exercises, and you've got a recipe for success.

#4871. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

#4870. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4869. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

I think it's really great that European consumer protection laws have a global impact because of the size of the European single market, and that they make life just a little bit easier for consumers all over the world. USB-C was just the beginning—there's more to come!

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4867. 9 Best Duvet Covers: Editor Sets to Style a Bedscape (2026)

Besides pieces like quilts and coverlets, I always say duvet covers are the best accessories to give a bedscape a bit more personality. Take it from Ariel Kaye, founder of juggernaut bedding brand Parachute, who has filled her eclectic LA home with a range of duvet covers that span vibrant, breezy linens to neutral, crisp percales.

To truly find the best of the best, I rounded up a group of writers and editors to test duvet covers from our favorite bedding brands—featuring muted, structured covers for minimalists and trendy colorways and patterns for maximalists. As for our top pick, we went with Boll & Branch’s Signature Hemmed Duvet Set since it’s organic, has a smooth and breathable feel, and comes in tons of prints and colors for easy styling.

If you’re still on the fence about what to go with for your bedroom, I also tapped AD PRO Directory designers to share what they look for in duvet covers, including materiality and design. Read below to create your dream bedscape this season.

For consistency, all prices listed reflect queen-size duvets unless otherwise noted, but up to king sizes are available for purchase from each brand.

Boll & Branch is one of AD’s favorite brands when it comes to bedding. With super soft sheets and other products made from 100% organic cotton, they have a heavy focus on sustainability and directly sourcing raw materials. The duvet cover follows suit, with long-staple cotton making for a durable piece of bedding that I’ve found is breathable enough for both hot and cold nights.

This organic-cotton duvet set can please pretty much anyone with a traditional bedroom. It has a tried-and-true cotton sateen material that gets softer with every wash, and designs—including subtle botanical prints—that are a must for anyone with classic taste. The earthy tones are great for a grounded bedroom too.

Bring the outdoors in with your styling by pairing one of Boll & Branch’s botanical prints with a textured linen sheet set.

Shop AD editors have stood behind Boll & Branch for years because of the brand’s sustainable business model and high-quality bedding. The signature cotton sheets have even earned a top spot in our best-of guides for the last five years. Just like these sheets, shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher tells me that this Boll & Branch duvet cover’s sateen weave has a buttery soft texture. “The cotton is very smooth, and I maintained a comfortable temperature throughout the night even when bundled up underneath all my bedding,” she says. As a cold sleeper, Arzbeacher loves layering extra throws and blankets on top of her duvet, and she says this ultra-breathable material has all the “cuddly qualities” you’d want without making you overheat. Even better, the bedding is 100% organic, so you can rest knowing you’re not breathing in any harmful chemicals.

This sateen duvet cover also has a zipper closure, so it’s a lot easier for Arzbaecher to slip her Company Store down insert on and off than other button-closure covers she’s tried. “Their solid color range has a lovely mix of earthy hues, and the brand has been releasing more and more patterns, from stripes to florals,” for styling a bed, she adds.

I’m not sure what’s left to say about this bedding brand that hasn’t already been plastered across subway ads or Instagram feeds, but in short, Brooklinen is somewhat of a bedding celebrity. It has garnered cool-kid status by offering top-quality products using Oeko-Tex-certified products at reasonable prices.

The Classic Duvet Cover is made of percale, which can be compared to a crisp cotton button-down shirt. It’s soft and sophisticated in a matte, buttery finish that can be attributed to long-staple cotton fibers that are spun to make stronger but finer yarn.

We are not only big fans of Brooklinen products for their breathable, sustainable materials but also for their versatile designs. With 20 earthy tones, I recommend this duvet cover for any type of bedroom style—but I’d lean towards purchasing for a coastal design because of the soothing colors and prints.

Like Alpert, who has this duvet cover in her bedroom, I recommend styling it with textured linen sheets for a contrasting yet comfortable fabric combination and a throw blanket in complementary neutral and oceanic hues.

Not one but two AD writers love this Brooklinen cotton duvet cover all year long. Shopping writer Julia Harrison calls this super, super soft and very cool to the touch. “It stays cool even when I’ve wrapped myself all the way in it like a caterpillar so I’m never overheating, but I am staying comfy and warm,” she shares. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert says this is her favorite duvet cover of all time, hands-down, because of its unmatched airy and parachute-like quality. “The percale duvet cover has this smooth feel but at the same time it is remarkably light and crisp,” she says. “Apparently, it’s all because of the high-quality single-ply yarns, which are made from strong, long-staple cotton fibers that give it that buttery touch.”

The style potential is a plus here too. Alpert loves the “oyster” print since it strays away from more expected patterns like stripes filling up her linen closet. She got the matching sheets in the same print for this exact reason, saying the swirls remind her of “Hokusai’s waves and stand out in the sea of florals and plaids” in her linen closet.

From pajamas to sheets, Cozy Earth is a favorite of ours—and Oprah thanks to frequent appearances in her Favorite Things lists—for cooling bedding made of bamboo fabric. Its offerings also ring in at a budget-friendly price (especially with the brand’s frequent sales).

Many of the colors in Cozy Earth’s collection are grounded in the earth (to be expected). With this in mind, I see this duvet cover in a minimalist, bohemian, or coastal bedroom. Alpert’s peony pick is just as nice for a romantic bedroom or something seasonal for summer.

The delicate nature of the bedding (both in texture and color) makes it a striking contrast against crisp, patterned accents, like a percale floral sheet set.

When I asked Alpert what her favorite qualities are about Cozy Earth’s signature, silky duvet cover, there were almost too many to count. “This duvet cover is a trifecta of perks: It looks good, feels good, and won’t slip off the comforter,” she says. “But if I had to pick one, I’d say that I love the delicate pink hue and the equally delicate feel of the cover—just looking at my bed makes me want to crawl into it.”

The material (100% viscose from bamboo) has a breathable and smooth feel to it that’s nice for hot sleepers but also anyone who doesn’t want a more textured cover like linen. Even better, the soft, pastel-inspired color options like peony pink and laurel green make it a great fit for styling a bed during this blooming season. “The fabric is so delicate and dreamy that it reminds me of flower petals,” Alpert tells me. “Since I chose the peony colorway, it definitely fits the romantic profile.”

Even though it has a smooth texture, the comforter inside won’t slip around because of the secure snap closures. “Cozy Earth has 12(!) points of contact between the comforter and the cover, so there is no way anything is going to get loose, especially because these are snapped on, and not tied, like many other duvet covers,” she says. “I pair it with the bamboo viscose comforter with standard fill and the combination works great because the comforter has some weight and the duvet cover does not mess with it in any way.”

A darling of the 2010s direct to consumer movement, Parachute is a home brand best known for its bedding, though the company has also dabbled in furniture, mattresses, and other essentials. This version, made of European Flax and made in the Guimarães region of Portugal, was inviting and oh so soft. The company also touts the material as naturally antimicrobial, which is a plus.

Another pick for a bohemian bedroom, this duvet cover has a lived-in look and several organic colors to choose from.

To Allen’s point, this means Parachute’s is more durable with a substantial feel and less opaque (the reason why she can’t see her duvet insert peeking through) with a lighter cover color like toast or sand.

Allen pairs her duvet cover with an all-season comforter from Riley, which she says stays secure through a button closure on the side and gives just the right amount of rumple together. The insert moves around a bit inside of the cover but mostly remains in place. “Best of all, I’ve been sleeping soundly with the set on hot nights as well as ones where the AC has been on overdrive, and so far it holds up in both situations—not too warm or cool.” Allen tells me that she shares a bed with her “hot-blooded husband and a large Maine Coon cat,” so her bed usually runs warm. This layerable, snuggly cover is perfect.

The home brand is headquartered in New York City, however, the materials are sourced from fourth-generation, family-owned textile mills in Portugal and other countries across Europe. The products span a range of bedding and bath products, namely duvet covers, sheets, towels, mats, and other accessories like pillows and robs.

Since all of the duvet covers come in neutral, unfussy colors, this is a great option for minimalists.

I style this simply with other neutrals like white or cream sheets. When I want to add more visual interest, I layer in butter yellow bedding or a quilt in soft, muted tones.

To put it simply, this duvet cover feels like a lightweight cashmere sweater. It’s not stuffy, but it’s not flimsy either. Even though it feels soft, it’s not made of pure cashmere. In reality, it’s made of 95% cotton and just 5% cashmere, but I wouldn’t have noticed if I didn’t read the label so closely. The texture has a brushed quality to it that feels gentle and light on my skin. There are a few neutral colors on the site. I went with the oatmeal and have liked styling it with white sheet sets so far for a simple, not-overly-done-up bedspread. Quince’s entire deal is about making high-quality luxury products at an affordable price. Quince is another AD favorite for its plethora of prints and solid colors. Try this duvet cover in your space—no matter its design style—for a lightweight addition to your bedscape that’s also budget friendly.

Since linen makes a statement on its own with its lived-in look, I recommend styling this duvet cover with Quince’s classic European linen sheet set and a fluffy duvet insert in moody neutral hues (think deep brown) for a cozy sleep oasis. It’s not as soft as something like an heirloom-quality stonewashed linen, but I’m not too picky in the linen department. I think its Oeko-Tex certification gives it a leg up generally to some competitors in this fabric category too.

I chose this Quince duvet since there were so many color options to choose from. I love moody colors year-round, and the burgundy is true to the deep color I saw on the site and it hasn’t faded after months of washes. It has the relaxed look you know and love with linen materials. Steaming it knocks out wrinkles easily whenever I want a more put-together look in my bedroom, though.

At this price point and with the most colors and prints available in this guide, I think this comforter cover can give you a great, budget-friendly way to dress a bed. The button closures also help keep a duvet insert or comforter in place. The care has been simple. I wash it with similar colors on a cold cycle and tumble dry on low and have only noticed a loose thread here and there, but nothing too crazy.

As mentioned above in our top overall pick, Brooklinen is known as the “home of the internet’s favorite sheets,” so we find it to be a worthy destination for quality bedding—including this quilt-like duvet cover made with 100% cotton.

Alpert thinks this material combo is genius since it keeps the duvet cover from feeling too heavy. “This is especially key for anyone who sleeps without a flat sheet—you’ll feel like you’re getting into freshly changed linens night after night,” she says. “On the flip side, the ribbed texture elevates the duvet cover, not only in how it looks but it gives your bedding a slightly cushy sensation.”

Rest assured that the feel isn’t as heavy as an actual weighted blanket. Alpert says it certainly has substance and structure, though. “When I sleep with it on, it feels as if I am very secure—no one will dare wake me up,” she notes.

Hommey is a relatively new Australian-based brand that got its start in 2020. It became popular for robes and nightwear in bold, fashionable stripes. The designs are now spread across the bedding category, including cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers.

Since the brand is known for more out-of-the-box colorways across its collections, this duvet color is a great option for maximalists looking to experiment with bold color-blocking.

For a moodier bedscape, I style this duvet cover with sheets in a deep tone like burgundy. Overall, the chocolatey hue acts like a neutral and pairs beautifully with lighter sheet colors like oatmeal, which can also complement the cream-colored trim.

I know we’ve talked about linen a couple of times already in this story, but Hommey’s duvet helps hit the trifecta for the category. The natural flax fiber felt smoother and more broken-in than my Quince version right out the package. My guess is that it’s because of the stonewashed finish, which is known to give scratchy linen a more silky quality. I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes. The duvet caught my attention even more because of all of the styles. There are over 30 fashionable colors and prints, like the oxford and plum reversible cotton duvet I want in a button-down shirt version. The linen offering has four distinct colorways, including the brown sugar with cream trim that I got for myself. I like deep colors for my bedscape, especially as the year starts inching towards fall and winter, and its rich hue hasn’t disappointed. It's the perfect complement to my autumnal color palette, especially when I pair it with burgundy linen sheets.

It is less expensive than the Parachute pick and has a plusher texture than the Quince, so I’d say this is the perfect middle ground for an approachable but high-quality linen duvet.

Garnet Hill was founded in New Hampshire in the mid-1970s by Pegge and Grant Dowse who built the brand on a commitment to sustainable materials, thoughtful craftsmanship, and responsible sourcing with products like organic cotton and flannel bedding. The bedding blends traditional styles with a modern touch to fit in a range of bedrooms.

Our tester says the Pear Garden print is completely unexpected. “As much as I love florals, stripes, and gingham, a girl needs a break…and these charming pears are just the right motif,” Alpert shares. “They signal a cottagecore moment without going over the top. Every time I glimpse the cheery yellow fruit, I crack a little smile. Plus, the colorway of bold yellow, sage green, brown, and cream are easy to coordinate with the rest of my bedding collection.”

Because the pear motifs are the statement, we think you can go with more subtle sheets like a white set with embroidered trim. If you’re more of a maximalist, you can lean into the pattern play with a gingham sheet set in a complementary muted tone like brown and extra layers like a faux fur blanket if you’re cozying up for winter.

According to Alpert, this duvet cover is synonymous with cozy. It’s the softest option on this list because of the brushed flannel fabric, and it’s also a great pick if you live in cold climates since it has a bit of heft to it. “It’s as if a layer of leaves, or in this case pears, is surrounding me during winter hibernation,” she says. “That’s in part because this specific flannel is woven to have a substantial six-ounce weight.”

Alpert’s had this for nearly one year and says it has a decadent texture, likening it to climbing under a layer of meringue when she pairs it with her fluffy Ostermoor down duvet insert. “The plush feel of the cover also makes me think that I’ve just scored an upgrade to a royal suite,” Alpert adds.

At this point, she hasn’t noticed any pilling, but she does note that the cover is a bit snugger than a typical king, so you can expect the duvet to feel a little loftier than a regular fit.

What to Look for in the Best Duvet Covers

A duvet cover is more than just a bedcover. This eye-catching textile has a large footprint in any bedroom and can instantly give your space a refresh—whether with unique colors and prints or something more modest—especially if you want to disguise an old duvet insert. With this in mind, I tapped AD PRO Directory designers to weigh in on what to look for in a duvet cover to elevate your bedroom.

Material: When it comes to duvet covers, everyone has their own personal preferences. For Nicole R. Fisher, CEO and founder of Nicole Fisher Interiors, it’s linen: “They’re effortless, lightweight, and airy. I think the simplicity of the linen transcends different styles and spaces,” she says. Fisher notes that the feel is a big factor when selecting a duvet cover.

Carmen René Smith, founder and principal designer of Aquilo Interiors, says that it also needs to feel soft to the touch, breathable, and cozy. “What’s the point of a beautiful duvet if you don’t want to snuggle into it?” she says. “Texture is key too—whether it’s silky, crisp, or nubby, it should add depth to the space.”

Comfort: All of the interior designers I spoke to for this story point to natural fibers, not only because of their quality but also their airflow and breathability. Shelbie Cox of Shelbie Cox Studio recommends natural fibers like organic cotton and linen and notes that polyester and other synthetic fibers are best to avoid since they can trap heat.

Design: With so many patterns and colors to choose from, it’s important to keep your bedroom’s design style in mind. If you like more of a minimalist bedroom, Cox suggests a fine stripe pattern (like Quince’s European Linen Duvet Cover) or a monochromatic, muted color palette (see the Cozy Earth Bamboo Duvet Cover) for your duvet cover set.

If you want to go bold for your bedroom, there are options aplenty. “We’re maximalists, so we say bump up the color and pattern no matter what your signature style is!” says Smith, adding that it’s important to still maintain balance. “If you have bold wallpaper, pull a color from it and go for a solid, textured duvet—like a rich velvet for drama or a soft linen for a more relaxed vibe. If you’re mixing patterns, think about scale—a bold, oversized print pairs best with a smaller, more delicate duvet pattern to give the eye a place to rest.”

If you don’t want to commit to one style just yet, rest assured that having a few duvets in rotation can help you keep your bedroom design fresh. “I tend to go simple on bedding and let the accessories be the pops of pattern and color that’s easily swapped out,” adds Fisher.

Maintenance: While these are great design accessories for a bedroom, they also need to be practical. Ashley Ross, founder and principal designer of Muse Noire Interiors recommends keeping these questions in mind when shopping: How does it fasten (zipper, tie up, or buttons)? Does it fit within your washer and dryer? This will help you know how to use it and how to care for it.

We tested the best duvet covers the same way we test products for the rest of our sleep content: by bringing the items in our homes and dressing them on our beds. This way, you’re guaranteed to get a real-life look at how the products perform after weeks and months of everyday use. We also wash them routinely to keep an eye out for any wear and tear. All of the brands we feature reflect a variety of price points, designs, and materials so you have the best options to choose from for your bedroom.

Jump to the “How We Tested” section of this article to watch an in-depth video about our testing methodology and some of our favorite products and brands.

You don’t necessarily need a duvet cover. It depends on how you like to dress your bed. In my opinion, it’s a great bed accessory. A duvet cover not only protects your duvet insert but it also gives you the opportunity to easily switch up your bedscape (instead of swapping comforters when you want a new look). That said, pay attention to the care instructions for your insert because some do not recommend washing or dry cleaning.

There are several ways you can put a duvet cover on, but according to TikTok experts, this method below is as foolproof as possible:

Start by turning your duvet cover inside out, top side down, with the duvet opener at the foot of the bed. Then, place your comforter on top and secure the corners with the attached ties to the duvet cover. Starting at the head of the bed, roll the duvet down towards the foot just like a burrito. Finally, fold the duvet opening over each end of the roll, and unroll the blanket back towards the

Always check the manufacturer instructions to find out how to wash your specific duvet cover. However, the most common way to clean a duvet cover is by machine washing it with like colors with a gentle detergent on a cold cycle. If the duvet cover has a zipper closure, it's usually helpful to zip it closed to keep it from snagging in the washing machine.

It's generally recommended to wash your duvet cover as often as you wash your sheets, which is about once a week. If you use a top sheet, though, you can usually extend another week and wash your duvet cover every other week.

Our editors selected top products in this story from tried-and-true brands on the market, from Brooklinen to Boll & Branch. These brands boast organic materials like 100% organic cotton and European Flax and bamboo for a sustainably made bed. Plus, many boast eco-friendly certifications like GOTS and Oeko-Tex so you know they are free of chemicals. As a design editor, I also made sure all of the products have a range of colors, patterns, and prints to complement a bedroom’s style.

#4866. After 471,625 miles, this Chevy Bolt is doing better than you think [video]

Wondering how long your new electric car might last? This 2019 Chevrolet Bolt EV is proving that electric vehicles can rack up miles with the best of them – and its owner is committed to taking it past the half million mile mark.

You’d think a 250,000 mile Ford Mustang Mach-E maintaining 92% of its battery life, a 360,000 mile Hyundai IONIQ 5 with 87% battery health still intact, and a half-dozen stories of Tesla Model S, 3, and Y ride share vehicles racking up six figures on their odometers later would do more to convince the slow adopters and doubting Thomases of the world that EV batteries are built to last. The good news is that the evidence keeps piling up, and this latest example of electric endurance is a good one.

On the Out of Spec Renew YouTube channel, the crew took in a 2019 Chevy Bolt EV – one of the most affordable new EVs you could buy in 2019 – that had more than 470,000 miles on the clock and 330,000 miles on its post-recall battery. That’s nearly half a million miles on the original electric motor, and it’s still got more to go.

Average gas car lasts ~150k miles. For sure requiring more maintenance to reach that mileage than an EV. Achieving ~500k on the original motor and over 300k on a battery is quite impressive.

Getting towards the 100k mile mark in both our EVs. Both feel like brand new and have required almost no maintenance - a fraction of what would be required with ICE. Look forward to hitting 200k and beyond in each. For the first time in over 30 years of driving, I don’t look forward to replacing our cars as they get over 100k miles - rather I look forward to the next 100k miles of driving.

Out of Spec Renew replaced the 2019’s battery pack that was experiencing serious battery faults and cell-voltage imbalances with a stable, lower-mile example from a 2017 model. Once it was up and in, they got the car powered up, programmed, and driving again, putting the owner on track to reach the 500,000 mile milestone (sorry) in their trusty steed.

The OOSR crew paid $1,800 for the “new” battery, but estimates consumers would pay between $2,500-3,000 for the a similar pack. You can check out the full battery replacement video, below, then let us know how far you plan on taking your EV in the comments.
